### 1.  Simplifying one factor  

Let  

\[
\theta_n=\frac{n\pi}{2n+1}\qquad (n\ge 1).
\]

Using  

\[
\frac{1+i\cot\theta}{1-i\cot\theta}=e^{2i\arctan(\cot\theta)},
\]

and \(\arctan(\cot \theta)=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\),

\[
\frac{1+i\cot\theta_n}{1-i\cot\theta_n}
 =e^{2i\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta_{n}\right)}
 =e^{i(\pi-2\theta_{n})}.
\]

But  

\[
\pi-2\theta_n
= \pi- \frac{2n\pi}{2n+1}
= \frac{\pi}{2n+1}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{1+i\cot\left(\frac{n\pi}{2n+1}\right)}{1-i\cot\left(\frac{n\pi}{2n+1}\right)}
= e^{\, i\pi/(2n+1)} .
\]

Raising this to the power \(1/n\) gives  

\[
\left(e^{\, i\pi/(2n+1)}\right)^{1/n}
= e^{\, i\pi/(n(2n+1))}.
\]

---

### 2.  The infinite product

\[
\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}
\left(\frac{1+i\cot\left(\frac{n\pi}{2n+1}\right)}{1-i\cot\left(\frac{n\pi}{2n+1}\right)}\right)^{1/n}
= \exp\!\left(i\pi\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(2n+1)}\right).
\]

Thus we need the series

\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n(2n+1)}.
\]

---

### 3.  Evaluating \(S\)

Use partial fractions:

\[
\frac{1}{n(2n+1)}=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{2}{2n+1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}-2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2n+1}.
\]

The harmonic series diverges, but the difference converges.  
Write the second sum over all odd integers:

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2n+1}
=\sum_{\substack{k=3\\ k\ \text{odd}}}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}
= \sum_{\substack{k=1\\ k\ \text{odd}}}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}-1 .
\]

Hence

\[
S
= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}
-2\!\left(\sum_{\text{odd }k}\frac{1}{k}-1\right)
= -\sum_{\text{odd }k}\frac{1}{k}
+2\sum_{ n\text{ even}}\frac{1}{n}+2 .
\]

The well–known identity

\[
\sum_{ \text{odd }k}\frac{1}{k}
-\sum_{ \text{even }n}\frac{1}{n}
 = \ln 2
\]

gives

\[
S = -( \ln 2 + \sum_{ \text{even }n}\frac{1}{n}) + \sum_{ \text{even }n}\frac{1}{n} + 2 = 2-\ln 2 .
\]

So

\[
\boxed{S = 2-\ln 2 } .
\]

---

### 4.  The value of the product

\[
\text{Product}
= \exp\!\bigl(i\pi(2-\ln 2)\bigr)
= e^{\,i2\pi}\,e^{-i\pi\ln 2}
= 1\cdot e^{-i\pi\ln 2}
= \exp\!\bigl(i\pi\ln(2^{-1})\bigr).
\]

Thus the product equals

\[
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\,i\pi}.
\]

Hence

\[
p=\;1,\qquad q=\;2,
\]

which are coprime.  

\[
p+q=1+2=3.
\]

Because \(a_{k-1},a_k ,a_{k+1}>0\), from (1)

Thus the odd–indexed terms are decreasing and so are the even–indexed

Also

\]

With (1) we obtain

\[
a _{\,k-1}a _{\,k+1}<a _{\,k-1}-a _{\,k+1}\tag{3}
\]

and consequently

\[
a _{\,k+1}<\frac{a _{\,k-1}}{\,a _{\,k-1}+1}\le 1 \qquad(k=1,\ldots ,n-1).
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A useful transformation

Put  

\[
b_k=\frac{1}{a_k}\qquad(k=0,1,\ldots ,n).                \tag{5}
\]

Dividing (1) by \(a_{k-1}a_k a_{k+1}\) and using (5) gives

\[
(b_{k-1}+b_k)(b_k+b_{k+1})=b_{k+1}-b_{k-1}\qquad (k=1,\ldots ,n-1).   \tag{6}
\]

Equation (6) is much simpler because it is linear in the differences
\(b_{k+1}-b_{k-1}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Telescoping in the transformed variables

Write (6) as

\[
b_{k+1}-b_{k-1}=(b_{k-1}+b_k)(b_k+b_{k+1})               \tag{7}
\]

and shift \(k\) successively.  
Add the relations for \(k=1,2,\ldots ,n-1\):

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(b_{k+1}-b_{k-1})
     =\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(b_{k-1}+b_k)(b_k+b_{k+1}) .
\tag{8}
\]

The left–hand side telescopes:

\[
(b_2-b_0)+(b_3-b_1)+\cdots +(b_n-b_{\,n-2})
          =b_n-b_0-b_{\,n-2}+b_1 .
\]

Using (2) we have \(b_1<b_0\) and \(b_{\,n-2}<b_{\,n-4}\),
so the left–hand side is a positive number.

\[

     \bigl(b_{\,n-2}-b_1\bigr) .
\tag{9}
\]

All terms on the right–hand side are non‑negative; moreover,
because of (4) we have \(a_k\le1\), whence \(b_k\ge1\).
Hence each product \((b_{k-1}+b_k)(b_k+b_{k+1})\) is at least

\[
b_n-b_0\ge 4(n-1)-\bigl(b_{\,n-2}-b_1\bigr)\ge 4(n-1)-2 .
\]

Consequently

\[
b_n\ge 4(n-1)-2+b_0 .
\]

Since \(b_0=1/a_0\ge1\),

\[

The differential equations
\[
\frac{dx}{yz}=\frac{dy}{zx}=\frac{dz}{xy}
\]
are equivalent to the following first‑order system  

\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{dx}{dt}=yz,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{dy}{dt}=zx,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{dz}{dt}=xy,
\end{cases}\qquad t\in \mathbb {R},
\]
which is obtained by cancelling a common infinitesimal \(dt\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Integrals of the system

Taking the ratio of the first two equations gives  

\[
\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{yz}{zx}=\frac{y}{x}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
x\,dx=y\,dy .
\]

Integrating,
\[
\frac{x^{2}}{2}=\frac{y^{2}}{2}+C_{1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_{1}=x^{2}-y^{2}.
\tag{1}
\]

Similarly, from the last two equations  

\[
\frac{dy}{dz}=\frac{zx}{xy}=\frac{z}{x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x\,dy=z\,dz
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
xz=y^{2}\!-\!C_{2},
\tag{2}
\]
and finally from the first and last equations

\[
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{xy}{yz}=\frac{x}{z}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
z\,dz=x\,dx
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
z^{2}=x^{2}+C_{3}.
\tag{3}
\]

Thus a complete set of independent integrals is

\[
\boxed{\,x^{2}-y^{2}=A,\qquad z^{2}=x^{2}+B\,}\qquad(A,B\in\mathbb{R}),
\]
or equivalently

\[
x^{2}-y^{2}=A,\qquad z^{2}-x^{2}=B .
\tag{4}
\]

### 2.  Surfaces through the circle \(\;x=0,\;y^{2}+z^{2}=1\)

Every point of the circle gives rise to a one‑parameter family of
integral curves.  The whole family of integral curves that meet the
circle is therefore the union of all surfaces \((4)\) for which
\(x=0,\;y^{2}+z^{2}=1\) is contained.

If a point on the circle \((0,y_{0},z_{0})\) belongs to one of the
surfaces, then from (4)

\[
x^{2}-y^{2}= -y_{0}^{2},\qquad z^{2}-x^{2}=z_{0}^{2}.
\]

Because \(y_{0}^{2}+z_{0}^{2}=1\), the constants \(A\) and \(B\) must
satisfy  

\[
A+ B = -\,y_{0}^{2}+z_{0}^{2}= -(1-z_{0}^{2})+z_{0}^{2}=z_{0}^{2}-1 .
\]

Eliminating \(A\) and \(B\) we obtain a single surface which contains
**every** integral curve that meets the circle:

\[
\boxed{\;x^{2}+\,y^{2}+\,z^{2}=1\;}
\]

Indeed, any point \((x,y,z)\) on the sphere satisfies the two first
integrals (with \(A=x^{2}-y^{2}\) and \(B=z^{2}-x^{2}\)), and for
\(x=0\) it reduces to \(y^{2}+z^{2}=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conclusion

The set of all integral curves of the given differential system that
intersect the circle \(x=0,\;y^{2}+z^{2}=1\) is the entire unit sphere

\[
\boxed{\;x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1\;}
\]

which is the surface generated by these solutions.

### 2.  Expressing \( \dfrac{AP}{PE}\) in terms of the barycentric
coefficients

Put \( \vec a=(a_{1},a_{2}),\;\vec b=(b_{1},b_{2}),\;\vec
c=(c_{1},c_{2})\).
The line \(AP\) is the set \(t\,\vec a\;(t\in\mathbb R)\).
The segment \(BC\) is described by  

\[

\]

We look for the point \(E\) where the two parameterisations meet, i.e.

\[
t\,\vec a=\vec b+\lambda(\vec c-\vec b).      \tag{2}
\]

The distance from \(P\) to \(E\) is \(|t\,\vec a|\) and the distance
\(AP\) equals \(|\vec a|\).  
Hence  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\frac{AP}{PE}=\frac{|\vec a|}{|t\,\vec a|}
      =\frac{1}{t}}\; . \tag{3}
\]

Thus we only have to minimise  \(t>0\) over all admissible triangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Unimodular invariants – the “lattice index’’  

Equation (2) has the unique solution  

\[
t=\frac{(\vec b\times\vec c)}{(\vec a\times\vec c)}
  =\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)}{(\vec a\times\vec c)},
\]

where \(u\times v=u_{1}v_{2}-u_{2}v_{1}\) is the 2‑dimensional
cross product (the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by
\(u,v\)).  

Because \(\vec b\times\vec c\) is the (signed) double area of
\(\triangle PBC\), the quantity \(|\vec b\times\vec c|\) is the
number of lattice points on the two sides \(PB\) and \(PC\) minus
1; the same holds for \(\vec a\times\vec c\) and the other two sides.
Using Pick’s theorem for the sub‑triangles, one finds

\[
|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec b\times\vec c|
=|\vec c\times\vec a| = B-2 ,        \tag{4}
\]

where \(B\) is the total number of lattice points on the boundary of
\(\triangle ABC\).  
(Indeed each boundary length consists of two lattice steps plus the
vertex that is common to the two adjacent sides.)

\[
t=\frac{B-2}{B-2}=1 ,
\]

impossible.  The mistake lies in forgetting that the three products
\(\vec a\times\vec b ,\,\vec b\times\vec c ,\,\vec c\times\vec a\)
are not all equal; only each pair of consecutive products is
congruent modulo \(B-2\).

\]

\]

then the triangle would have area \(1/2\) and contain no interior

Because \( \dfrac{AP}{PE}=1/t\), a smaller \(t\) gives a larger ratio.
From the previous paragraph the smallest attainable \(t\) is \(1/4\).
Hence

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\max \frac{AP}{PE}=4 } .
\]

### 6.  Conclusion

The maximal possible value of \( \dfrac{AP}{PE}\) for a lattice
triangle containing exactly one interior lattice point is **4**,
and this value is achieved, for instance, by the triangle with vertices

In 0.10 L of water 0.01 mol of each component is present, so that the initial concentrations are

\[

The OH⁻ of NaOH reacts with the acidic form of the carbonate system:

\[
\mathrm{H_2CO_3 + OH^- \;\longrightarrow\; HCO_3^- + H_2O}
\]

Since there are 0.10 M of OH⁻ and 0.10 M of H₂CO₃, the reaction goes to completion.  
After the reaction has finished:

* The \(0.10\;{\rm M}\) H₂CO₃ is completely consumed.
* The amount of HCO₃⁻ increases by 0.10 M (from the conversion of H₂CO₃) while the original 0.10 M NaHCO₃ remains.
* No OH⁻ is left.

In the absence of other species, the equilibria that control the pH are

\[
\mathrm{HCO_3^- \;\rightleftharpoons\; H^+ + CO_3^{2-}}

\[

For a buffer containing the conjugate acid \( \mathrm{HCO_3^-}\) and conjugate base \( \mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\), the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is

\[
\boxed{\;pH = pK_{a2} + \log \frac{[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}\;}

Let a convex polyhedron \(P\) have a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with the usual Euler relation  

\[
|V|-|E|+|F|=2,\qquad\qquad(\star)
\]

Let \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) be the two closed walks (Hamiltonian
circuits) travelled by the first and the second ant.  
For a face \(F\in\mathcal F(P)\) denote

\[
t_i(F)=\#\{\,e\in F\cap C_i\,\}\qquad(i=1,2)
\]

(the number of edges of \(F\) that belong to the \(i\)-th route).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A linear equality

Count the incidences “edge–face of the walk’’ in two ways.
Each edge of a walk belongs to exactly two faces, hence

\[
\sum_{F\in\mathcal F(P)}t_i(F)=2\,|C_i|\qquad(i=1,2).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Equality of the two walks outside one face

Assume that there is exactly one face \(F^{*}\) for which  

\[
t_1(F^{*})\neq t_2(F^{*}),
\tag{2}
\]

and for every \(F\ne F^{*}\),

\[
t_1(F)=t_2(F).
\tag{3}
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{F\in\mathcal F(P)}t_1(F)-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F(P)}t_2(F)
      =t_1(F^{*})-t_2(F^{*})
      =:d\neq 0 .          
\tag{4}
\]

On the other hand, after applying (1) to \(i=1,2\),

\[
\sum_{F}t_1(F)-\sum_{F}t_2(F)=2(|C_1|-|C_2|).
\tag{5}
\]

Hence

\[
d=2(|C_1|-|C_2|).                                           
\tag{6}
\]

So the difference \(d\) is an even integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The value of \(d\) must be odd

Consider the walk \(C_1\).  
Because \(C_1\) does not visit a vertex twice, at each vertex it
enters and leaves through two distinct edges; thus every vertex of
\(G\) is incident with an **even number** of edges of \(C_1\).
Consequently the degree of every vertex in the subgraph
\((V,C_1)\) is even.  The same holds for \(C_2\).

Now look at the subgraph \((V,C_1\triangle C_2)\) obtained by taking
the symmetric difference of the two edge sets.  
Each vertex of this subgraph has odd degree (because it is the sum of
two even degrees modulo 2).  A graph in which all vertices have odd
degree has an **odd** number of edges.  Therefore

\[
|C_1\triangle C_2| \text{ is odd}.
\tag{7}
\]

But

\[
|C_1\triangle C_2|=|C_1|+|C_2|-2|C_1\cap C_2|
                 =|C_1|-|C_2|\quad(\text{mod }2),
\]

so \( |C_1|-|C_2|\) is odd.  
Hence by (6) the difference \(d\) is also **odd**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Contradiction

Equation (6) shows that \(d\) is even, while (7) shows that \(d\) is
odd – a contradiction.  Therefore assumption (2) cannot hold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

There is **no** convex polyhedron together with two Hamiltonian
routes as described such that all faces contain the same pair of
numbers except for exactly one face.  In other words, for any two
ant‑routes of the kind required, at least two faces must differ in the
pair of numbers they carry. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Hence the answer to the problem is “No’’ – an example does not
exist.**

\]

and we write

\qquad
\mathbf{v}_6 = y\!\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)
\]

for the unknown lengths $x=DE$ and $y=EF$.

\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2+\mathbf{v}_3+\mathbf{v}_4+

\]

Taking the $x$– and $y$–components gives the linear system

\[
\begin{cases}
6+4-5-12-\dfrac{x}{2}+\dfrac{y}{2}=0,\\[0.3cm]
4\sqrt3+5\sqrt3-\dfrac{x\sqrt3}{2}-\dfrac{y\sqrt3}{2}=0,
\end{cases}
\]

from which

\]

### The eight vertices

Starting at $A=(0,0)$ and successively adding the side vectors we obtain the coordinates    

\[
\begin{aligned}
A &= (0,0),\\
B &= (6,0),\\
C &= (10,\,4\sqrt3),\\
D &= (5,\,9\sqrt3),\\
E &= (-7,\,9\sqrt3),\\
F &= (-8,\,8\sqrt3).
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### The incenter

Let $(h,k)$ be the point which is equidistant from all six sides.
For an equiangular hexagon the interior angles are all $120^\circ$,
hence the inward normal of each side is perpendicular to the side vector.
Hence for each side we can write the (oriented) line equation
and we obtain that $(h,k)$ must satisfy

\[
\begin{aligned}
k &= r,\\
-\;{\sqrt3}\,(h-6)+4(k-0) &= r,\\
-\,{\sqrt3}\,(h-10)-5(k-4\sqrt3) &= r,\\
\dots
\end{aligned}
\]

Eliminating $h$ and $k$ gives the common distance $r$ from $(h,k)$ to
any side.  Solving the system yields

\[
r=5\sqrt3 .
\]

So the diameter of the incircle is

\[
d=2r=10\sqrt3 ,
\qquad d^2=(10\sqrt3)^2=300 .
\]

\end{cases}
\]

Hence the potential \(V(r)\) (choosing \(V(\infty)=0\)) is obtained from  

\[
V(r)=-\int_{\infty}^{\,r}\mathbf E\!\cdot d\mathbf l .
\]

---

### 1.  Outside the sphere  \((r\ge R)\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
V(r) &=
-\int_{\infty}^{\,R}\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} r^{2}}\,dr
-\int_{R}^{\,r}\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} r^{2}}\,dr\\[4pt]
&=0+\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} r}
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\,V_{\text{out}}(r)=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}\, r}\qquad (r\ge R)\,}
\]

---

### 2.  Inside the sphere  \((r<R)\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
V(r) &= V_{\text{out}}(R)-\int_{R}^{\,r}\mathbf E\!\cdot d\mathbf l\\[4pt]
&= \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}
-\int_{R}^{\,r}\frac{Q r'}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{3}}\;dr'\\[4pt]

-\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{3}}
\,\frac{r^{2}-R^{2}}{2}\\[6pt]
&= \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}\;
\Bigl(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\Bigr)
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\,V_{\text{in}}(r)=
\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}\,
\left(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\right)
\qquad (r<R)\,}
\]

---

**Summary**

\[
V(r)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}\,
\displaystyle\Bigl(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\Bigr) & (r<R),\\[12pt]
\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0} r} & (r\ge R).
\end{cases}
\]

A(0,0),\qquad B(s,0),\qquad C(s,s),\qquad D(0,s)
\]

Point \(E\) lies on \(AD\), so \(E=(0,y)\) with \(0<y<s\).
Point \(F\) lies on \(BC\), so \(F=(s,z)\) with \(0<z<s\).

The given equalities of distances give

\[
\begin{cases}
BE^2 = s^{2}+y^{2}=30^{2}=900\\[4pt]
EF^2 = s^{2}+(z-y)^{2}=900\\[4pt]
FD^2 = s^{2}+ (z-s)^{2}=900
\end{cases}
\]

---

### 1. Relation between \(y\) and \(z\)

Subtract the first two equations:

\[
(z-y)^{2}-y^{2}=0 \implies (z-y)^{2}=y^{2}\implies |z-y|=|y|
\]
Since \(y\ge 0,\;z\ge 0\), this yields  
\(z=2y\) (the alternative \(z=0\) would force \(y\ge s\), impossible).

---

### 2. Relation between \(z\) and \(s\)

Subtract the last two equations:

\[
(z-s)^{2}-(z-y)^{2}=0\implies |z-s|=|z-y|
\]

Because \(z\le s\), \(|z-s|=s-z\).  
There are two possibilities:

* \(s-z=z-y\)  \(\Longrightarrow\)  \(y=2z-s\)
* \(s-z=-(z-y)\)  \(\Longrightarrow\)  \(y=s\) (impossible because then \(z=2y> s\))

Thus \(y=2z-s\).

Substitute \(z=2y\):

\[
y=2(2y)-s \Longrightarrow y=4y-s \Longrightarrow 3y=s
\]

Hence

\[
y=\frac{s}{3},\qquad z=2y=\frac{2s}{3}
\]

---

### 3. Determine \(s\)

Insert \(y=\dfrac{s}{3}\) into the first distance equation:

\[
s^{2} + \left(\frac{s}{3}\right)^{2}=900
\;\Longrightarrow\;
s^{2}+\frac{s^{2}}{9}=900
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{10}{9}s^{2}=900
\;\Longrightarrow\;
s^{2}=900\cdot \frac{9}{10}=810
\]

So the side length is \(s=\sqrt{810}=9\sqrt{10}\).

\]

\[

\]

### 3.  Existence of a solution

Define for \(t\in[0,1]\)

\[
x_{i}^{(t)} = a + t\,\frac{(b-a)i}{n}, \qquad i=0,\dots ,n,
\tag{7}
\]
so that \(x^{(0)}_{i}=a\) (degenerate partition) and
\(x^{(1)}_{i}=a+\frac{(b-a)i}{n}\) is an equidistributed partition.
For each \(m\) put  

\[
\Phi_m(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i}\Bigl(\bigl(x_{i}^{(t)}\bigr)^{\,m+1}
-\bigl(x_{i-1}^{(t)}\bigr)^{\,m+1}\Bigr).
\]

The functions \(\Phi_m(t)\) are continuous on \([0,1]\).

* For \(t=0\) all \(x_{i}^{(0)}=a\) and, consequently, every term in

  \(\Phi_m(1)=0\) as well.

by the Intermediate Value Theorem we may sharpen the construction as
follows: at each step \(t_k=\frac{k}{n-1}\) we adjust only one point
\(x_{j}\) continuously until all \(\Phi_m(t_k)\) vanish simultaneously.
A standard argument of the *bisection method in several variables*
(or, equivalently, the implicit function theorem applied to
\(F=(\Phi_0,\dots ,\Phi_{n-1})\)) guarantees the existence of
\(t\in[0,1]\) for which simultaneously

\[
\Phi_m(t)=0,\qquad m=0,\dots ,n-1.
\]

Taking the corresponding partition \(x_{i}=x_{i}^{(t)}\) gives a
solution of the system (6), and thus (2).  
Consequently, for this partition

\[
\int_{x_{0}}^{x_{1}}f+\int_{x_{2}}^{x_{3}}f+\cdots
        =\int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}f+\int_{x_{3}}^{x_{4}}f+\cdots
\]
for every polynomial \(f\) of degree \(<n\).

### 4.  Conclusion

For every interval \([a,b]\) and every positive integer \(n\) there
exists a positive integer \(k\) (for instance \(k=n\)) and a partition
\(a=x_{0}<x_{1}<\dots <x_{k}=b\) that satisfies  

\[
\sum_{i\ {\rm odd}}\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}f=
\sum_{i\ {\rm even}}\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}f ,
\qquad\forall\, f\in\mathcal{P}_{n-1}.
\]

Thus the required partition exists for all intervals and all
\(n\). ∎

The neighbour on the left of \(k\) is \(k-1\) (indices modulo \(n\)).

At each minute all persons reply simultaneously and, afterwards, **adopt the answer they gave**.  
Hence the update rule is:

\[
x_k(t+1)=
\begin{cases}
x_{k-1}(t)      &\text{if }x_k(t)=1 \quad (\text{truthful})\\[2mm]
1-x_{k-1}(t)    &\text{if }x_k(t)=0 \quad (\text{liar}).
\end{cases}
\]

A simple algebraic manipulation gives the equivalent form  

\[
\boxed{\,x_k(t+1)=1 \iff x_{k-1}(t)=x_k(t)\,}\tag{1}
\]

Thus a person becomes truthful iff his left neighbour **has the same type** as him; otherwise he becomes a liar.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A convenient invariant

Let us look at any product of adjacent pairs

\[
P_k(t)=x_k(t)\oplus x_{k-1}(t)\qquad (\oplus=\text{exclusive OR}).
\]

From (1) we deduce immediately that

\[
x_k(t+1)=1-P_k(t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x_{k-1}(t+1)=1-P_{k-1}(t).
\]

Hence the new neighbouring differences satisfy

\[
P_k(t+1)=x_k(t+1)\oplus x_{k-1}(t+1)=
(1-P_k(t))\oplus(1-P_{k-1}(t))=P_k(t)\oplus P_{k-1}(t).
\tag{2}
\]

Iterating (2) shows that each \(P_k(t)\) is a **linear combination (over \(\mathbb F_2\)) of the initial differences**  
\(P_j(0)=x_j(0)\oplus x_{j-1}(0)\).  
Consequently the vector \(P(t)=(P_0(t),\dots ,P_{n-1}(t))\) evolves by a linear cellular‑automaton that is the well‑known *Rule 90*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Small values of \(n\)

*For \(n=1\).*  
There is only one person, his left neighbour is himself.  
Equation (1) gives \(x_0(t+1)=1\) for any \(x_0(t)\); after one step the only person is truthful forever.  
So \(n=1\) works.

*For \(n=2\).*  
Let the two persons be \(x_0,x_1\).  
The update rule (1) gives the system

\[
x_0(t+1)=1\iff x_0(t)=x_1(t),\qquad
x_1(t+1)=1\iff x_1(t)=x_0(t).
\]

A quick inspection of the four initial states shows that the only non‑stable orbit is  
\(00\to 11\).  
All possible initial configurations reach the all‑truthful state, which is therefore permanent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Why \(n\ge 3\) fails

Take \(n=3\) and the initial state \(x=(0,1,0)\) (liar, truthful, liar).  
Using (1) we get the successive states

\[
(0,1,0)\;\longrightarrow\;(1,0,0)\;\longrightarrow\;(0,0,1)\;\longrightarrow\;(0,1,0),
\]

a **cycle of length 3** that never reaches the all‑truthful configuration.  
Since the rule (1) is deterministic and translation‑invariant, such a cycle means that *for \(n=3\) the process is not guaranteed to converge to all truthful*.

A similar phenomenon occurs for any \(n\ge 3\).  
Indeed, consider the configuration where the people alternate between liar and truthful:

\[
x_k(0)= 
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if }k\text{ is even},\\
1 & \text{if }k\text{ is odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

If \(n\) is odd, this configuration is a fixed point of the rule (1).  
If \(n\) is even, it becomes a period‑2 orbit.  
In either case the all‑truthful state is unreachable from that initial configuration.

Thus **for every \(n\ge 3\) there exists at least one initial assignment that never becomes all‑truthful**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

The largest \(n\) for which **every** initial distribution of liars and truthful people inevitably converges (and then stays) to the all‑truthful configuration is

\[
\boxed{\;n_{\max}=2\;}.
\]

For \(n=1\) and \(n=2\) the desired property holds, while for every \(n\ge3\) it does not.

\[
(\sin*f)(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\sin t\,f(x-t)\,dt .

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Laplace transform

For \(x\ge 0\) take Laplace transforms.
\[
\mathcal L\{(\sin*f)(x)\}= \mathcal L\{f(x)\}\,\mathcal L\{\sin x\}
      =F(s)\frac{1}{s^{2}+1},
\]
and 
\[
\mathcal L\{f(x)-\sin x\}=F(s)-\frac{1}{s^{2}+1}.
\]

Hence the given equation transforms to  

\[
\frac{F(s)}{s^{2}+1}=F(s)-\frac{1}{s^{2}+1}.
\]

Rearranging,

\[
F(s)- (s^{2}+1)F(s) = -1
\Longrightarrow -s^{2}F(s)=-1
\Longrightarrow F(s)=\frac{1}{s^{2}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Inverse Laplace

\[
\mathcal L^{-1}\!\left\{\frac{1}{s^{2}}\right\}=x .
\]

Thus  
\[
f(x)=x,\qquad x\ge 0 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Verification for all real \(x\)

Take \(f(x)=x\) for all real \(x\) and compute for arbitrary \(x\)

\[
\int_{0}^{x} \sin t \,(x-t)\,dt
=x\int_{0}^{x}\sin t\,dt-\int_{0}^{x}t\sin t\,dt
=x(1-\cos x)-(-x\cos x+\sin x)=x-\sin x .
\]

Hence

\[
(\sin*f)(x)=x-\sin x=f(x)-\sin x,
\]

which is exactly the required relation.  
Since the function \(f(x)=x\) is continuous everywhere, it is the unique
continuous function satisfying the identity.

First rewrite the inner alternating series:

\[
\frac{1}{(n+1)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(n+2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(n+3)^{2}}-\dots
   =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{\,m-1}\frac{1}{(n+m)^{2}} .
\]

The whole sum is therefore

\[
S=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}
   (-1)^{m-1}\frac{1}{(n+m)^{2}}
   =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{m-1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
    (-1)^{n}\frac{1}{(n+m)^{2}}\!.
\]

Put \(r=n+m\) (\(n=r-m\)).  Then

\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{1}{(n+m)^{2}}
  =(-1)^{-m}\sum_{r=m}^{\infty}(-1)^{r}\frac{1}{r^{2}}
  =(-1)^{m}\sum_{r=m}^{\infty}(-1)^{r}\frac{1}{r^{2}} .
\]

Hence

\[
S=-\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\sum_{r=m}^{\infty}(-1)^{r}\frac{1}{r^{2}} .
\]

Swap the order of summation:

\[
S=-\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{r}\frac{1}{r^{2}}\,
   \underbrace{\sum_{m=1}^{r}1}_{=\,r}
   =-\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}r\frac{(-1)^{r}}{r^{2}}
   =-\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{r}}{r}
   =\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{\,r-1}}{r}\!.
\]

The last series is the well‑known alternating harmonic series:

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{\,r-1}}{r}=\ln 2 .
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\,S=\displaystyle\ln 2\, } .
\]

### 1.  A convenient change of variables  

Set  

\[
u=xy ,\qquad v=\frac{x}{y}\;(>0).
\]

Because \((x,y)\mapsto(u,v)\) is a diffeomorphism on \((1,\infty)^{2}\),
every twice–continuously differentiable \(f\) can be regarded as a function
\(F(u,v)\) of the new variables.
Let  

\[
f(x,y)=F(u,v)=F(xy,\tfrac{x}{y}).
\]

A short computation gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x f_{x}+y f_{y}
&=x\Bigl(F_{u}\,y+F_{v}\,\frac{1}{y}\Bigr)+
  y\Bigl(F_{u}\,x-F_{v}\,\frac{1}{x}\Bigr) \\[3pt]
&=2uF_{u}(u,v),                                         \\
x^{2}f_{xx}+y^{2}f_{yy}
&=2u^{2}F_{uu}(u,v),
                                               \end{aligned}
\]
and the mixed derivatives in \(u,v\) vanish because
\(u\) and \(v\) are independent.

Hence (A)–(B) become  

\[
\tag{A'} 2u F_{u}(u,v)=u\ln u ,\qquad
\tag{B'} 2u^{2} F_{uu}(u,v)=u .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Determining \(F\)

From (A') we obtain  

\[
F_{u}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\ln u \qquad(\forall\,u\ge 1,\;v>0).
\]

Integrating with respect to \(u\) gives  

\[
F(u,v)=\frac{u}{2}\!\bigl(\ln u-1\bigr)+H(v),
\]
where \(H\) is an arbitrary smooth function of \(v\).

Now \(F_{uu}=\dfrac{1}{2u}\);
substituting in (B') gives  

\[
2u^{2}\Bigl(\frac{1}{2u}\Bigr)=u ,
\]
which is an identity.  
Thus every \(H(v)\) is admissible; the family of solutions is

\[
\boxed{\,f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{2}\bigl(\ln(xy)-1\bigr)+ H\!\Bigl(\frac{x}{y}\Bigr)\, }.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing the discrete second difference  

For an integer \(s\ge1\) set  

\[
D(s)=f(s+1,s+1)-f(s+1,s)-f(s,s+1)+f(s,s).
\]

With the representation of \(f\) above,

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(s+1,s+1)&=\frac{(s+1)^{2}}{2}\bigl( \ln (s+1)^{2}-1\bigr)+H(1),\\[3pt]
f(s+1,s)&=\frac{s(s+1)}{2}\bigl( \ln (s(s+1))-1\bigr)+H\!\Bigl(1+\frac1s\Bigr),\\[3pt]
f(s,s+1)&=\frac{s(s+1)}{2}\bigl( \ln (s(s+1))-1\bigr)+H\!\Bigl(\frac{s}{s+1}\Bigr),\\[3pt]
f(s,s)&=\frac{s^{2}}{2}\bigl(\ln s^{2}-1\bigr)+H(1).
\end{aligned}
\]

A straightforward cancellation of all terms containing \(H\) occurs
(the terms \(H(1)\) cancel and the terms \(H(1+1/s)\) and
\(H(s/(s+1))\) are equal because \(1+1/s=s/(s+1)\)).
Thus

\[
D(s)=\frac{(s+1)^{2}}{2}\bigl(\ln (s+1)^{2}-1\bigr)
     -s(s+1)\bigl(\ln (s(s+1))-1\bigr)
     +\frac{s^{2}}{2}\bigl(\ln s^{2}-1\bigr).
\]

A bit of algebra using \(\ln (ab)=\ln a+\ln b\) gives

\[
\boxed{\,D(s)=\frac12\qquad (\forall\,s\ge1)\, }.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The minimum

Because \(D(s)=1/2\) for every allowed integer \(s\),

\[
m(f)=\min_{s\ge1} D(s)=\frac12,
\]

independent of the particular choice of
\(f\in\mathcal F\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion  

For every twice–continuously differentiable function
\(f\) satisfying the two differential equations, the quantity

\[
f(s+1,s+1)-f(s+1,s)-f(s,s+1)+f(s,s)
\]

is identically \(1/2\).  Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,m(f)=\dfrac12\,}
\]

and this value is the same for all functions in \(\mathcal F\).

The geometric sum evaluates to

\[

\[

\]

### Why 2017 is enough

The board can be viewed as the bipartite graph \(K_{2017,2017}\):  
Left–hand side vertices are the rows, right–hand side vertices are the columns, and each square is an edge connecting its row and its column.

Placing a coin is the same as choosing an edge of that graph, with the restriction that no two chosen edges share a vertex (the same row or column).  
The game therefore lasts exactly as long as the largest possible set of pairwise‑non‑adjacent edges, i.e. the size of a maximum matching in the graph.

* Without any forbidden squares the graph is the complete bipartite graph \(K_{2017,2017}\).  
  Its maximum matching has size \(2017\); hence Zandre (the first player) makes the
  1st, 3rd, …, 2017th moves and wins.

* By forbidding certain squares we delete edges from the graph.  
  We want to delete *as few* edges as possible so that the maximum matching drops to **even** (so that the second player, Andile, makes the last move).

---

### Minimising deleted edges

For a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover (Kőnig’s theorem).  
Hence we seek the smallest number of edges which must be removed so that the minimum vertex cover has size \(2016\) instead of \(2017\).

A vertex cover of size \(2016\) can be constructed in the following way:

1. Pick a *row* \(R\).  
2. Delete all edges incident to \(R\).  
   That is, forbid all \(2017\) squares in that row.

After these deletions the remaining graph is \(K_{2016,2017}\).  
Its minimum vertex cover has size \(\min(2016,2017)=2016\), so the maximum matching has size \(2016\) (even).  

Consequently, Andile, who moves second, will place the 2016th coin and win.

---

### Why fewer than 2017 forbidden squares cannot suffice

Suppose we delete \(k<2017\) edges.  
Then at least one row still has at least one free square, and at least one column still has at least one free square.  
The graph still contains a sub‑graph isomorphic to \(K_{1,1}\) (a single free square).  
Because all other rows and columns are still connected, a perfect matching for the whole \(2017 \times 2017\) bipartite graph remains possible: we can still match the remaining 2016 rows and 2016 columns together and match the remaining single row to the remaining single column.  

Thus, with fewer than \(2017\) forbidden squares, the maximum matching size remains \(2017\), odd, and Zandre still wins.

Hence **2017** is both necessary and sufficient.

Let the country be split into \(k\) regions.
Denote by  

* \(N\) the total number of employees in the country,
* \(S\) the total salary paid in the country,
* for region \(i\;(i=1,\dots ,k)\)  
  \(N_i\) – number of employees in that region  
  \(S_i\) – total salary paid in that region.

By assumption all employees satisfy

\[
\frac{N}{10}\;(\text{the top }10\%\text{ of all employees})\quad\text{receive}\quad 
\frac{9}{10}S\quad(\text{the top }90\%\text{ of the total salary}).
\]

---

### What the property of each region implies

The statement in the question reads

> “in every region the total salary of any 10 % of the employees is no greater than 11 % of the total salary paid in that region”

which means for every \(i\)

\[
\max_{\substack{A\subseteq\{1,\dots ,N_i\}\\|A|=0.1\,N_i}}
\frac{\sum_{j\in A} \text{salary}_j }{S_i}\le 0.11 ,
\]

or, in other words, the highest–earning \(10\%\) of the workers of region \(i\) earn **at most** \(11\%\) of the salary paid inside that region.  
Consequently the best‑possible salary that can be collected from the top \(10\%\) of employees in **any** region is bounded by \(0.11 S_i\).

---

### Summing the bounds over all regions

Let \(T\) be the sum of the salaries of the top \(10\%\) of all employees in the whole country.
We can obtain \(T\) by taking, for each region \(i\), the salaries of the richest \(10\%\) of that region (or a subset thereof) and summing across regions.  
Since in every region the richest \(10\%\) earn at most \(0.11 S_i\),

\[
T \;\le\; \sum_{i=1}^{k} 0.11\,S_i
      \;=\; 0.11\,\sum_{i=1}^{k} S_i
      \;=\; 0.11\,S .
\]

Thus the total salary paid to the top \(10\%\) of employees in the entire country cannot exceed **11 %** of the total salary.

---

### Impossible to reach the required 90 %

But the hypothesis of the problem requires that the top \(10\%\) of employees receive **90 %** of the total salary, i.e. \(T = 0.90\,S\).

The inequality we just proved gives \(T \le 0.11\,S\).  
Since \(0.90\,S>0.11\,S\), the two conditions cannot both be true.

Hence the stated situation is **impossible**. There is no way to divide a country into regions so that each region satisfies the “10 % of employees can earn at most 11 % of the region’s salary’’ rule while the entire country has 10 % of employees earning 90 % of the country’s salary.

Denote

The conditions that both swimmers reach \(P\) in the same time \(t\) are

\[

v_{y}\,t          &=264 .

### (a) Divisibility by \(73\)

Compute the inverse of \(9\) modulo \(73\).

\[
9^{-1}\equiv 65 \pmod{73}\qquad(9\cdot65=585\equiv1).
\]

Hence

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1} 2\cdot10^{i+2}
\equiv 2\cdot10^{2}\cdot \frac{10^{t}-1}{9}
\equiv 54\cdot65\,(10^{t}-1)
\equiv 6\,(10^{t}-1)\pmod{73}.
\]

With \(x=10^{t}\) we get

\[
N_{t}\equiv (27a+10b+6)\,x+25\pmod{73}. \tag{1}
\]

The number \(10^{t}\pmod{73}\) can take **many different values** (the period of \(10\) mod \(73\) is 8, but the first 16 powers are already distinct).  
Thus (1) must hold for all possible residues \(x\).

The only way for (1) to be identically zero for every \(x\) in that set is

\[
27a+10b+6\equiv 0\pmod{73}\qquad\text{and}\qquad 25\equiv 0\pmod{73}.
\]

The second congruence is impossible.  
Hence **there are no decimal digits \(a,b\)** such that every number of the
given form is divisible by \(73\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### (b) Divisibility by \(79\)

Now find the inverse of \(9\) modulo \(79\):

\[
9^{-1}\equiv 44 \pmod{79}\qquad(9\cdot44=396\equiv1).
\]

Thus

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1} 2\cdot10^{i+2}
\equiv 2\cdot10^{2}\,\frac{10^{t}-1}{9}
\equiv 42\cdot44\,(10^{t}-1)
\equiv 31\,(10^{t}-1)\pmod{79}. 
\]

Let again \(x=10^{t}\pmod{79}\).  Using \(10^{2}\equiv21\) we get

\[
N_{t}\equiv (21a+10b+31)\,x \pmod{79}. \tag{2}
\]

Notice that in (2) the *constant term* is already zero, so we only have to
force the coefficient of \(x\) to vanish for all possible residues
\(x\).  
Therefore we need

\[
21a+10b+31\equiv 0\pmod{79}. \tag{3}
\]

Searching for decimal digits \(a,b\in\{0,1,\dots ,9\}\) solving (3):

* compute \(21a\pmod{79}\) for \(a=0,\dots ,9\);
* use that \(10^{-1}\equiv8 \pmod{79}\) (since \(10\cdot8=80\equiv1\));
* for each \(a\) evaluate  
  \(10b\equiv -21a-31 \pmod{79}\).

Carrying this out gives one valid solution:

\[
a=6,\qquad b=8.
\]

Indeed,

\[
21\cdot6+10\cdot8+31=126+80+31=237\equiv 0\pmod{79}.
\]

Thus for **\(c=6,\;d=8\)** every integer of the form  
\(cd\,222\ldots 231\) is divisible by \(79\).

Let a parcel of air be in hydrostatic equilibrium in the Earth’s gravitational field.  
At a height \(Z\) above the Earth’s surface the pressure is \(p(Z)\).

---

### 1.  Hydrostatic balance

For a layer of thickness \(dZ\) the upward force exerted by the air below it must equal the weight of that layer:

\[
\frac{dp}{dZ}=-\rho \, g ,
\]

where  

* \(\rho(Z)\) – mass density of the air at height \(Z\),  
* \(g\) – (approximately constant) acceleration of gravity,  
* \(p\) – pressure.

---

### 2.  Ideal‑gas relation (isothermal atmosphere)

Assume the temperature \(T\) is constant with altitude (isothermal atmosphere).  
The ideal–gas law for a perfect gas reads

\[
p = \rho \frac{R\,T}{M} ,
\]

or equivalently  

\[
\rho = \frac{M}{R\,T}\,p ,
\]

with  

* \(M\) – molar mass of the air,  
* \(R\) – universal gas constant.

Insert this expression for \(\rho\) into the hydrostatic equation:

\[
\frac{dp}{dZ} = -\frac{M}{R\,T}\,p\, g .
\]

---

### 3.  Solve the differential equation

Rearrange:

\[
\frac{1}{p}\,dp = -\frac{M g}{R\,T}\, dZ .
\]

Integrate from sea level (where \(Z = 0,\;p = p_0\)) to an arbitrary height \(Z\):

\[
\int_{p_0}^{p(Z)} \frac{1}{p}\,dp
   = -\frac{M g}{R\,T}\int_{0}^{Z} dZ .
\]

\[
\ln\!\bigl(\tfrac{p(Z)}{p_0}\bigr) = -\frac{M g}{R\,T}\,Z .
\]

Exponentiate:

\[
\boxed{\,p(Z)=p_0 \exp\!\left(-\,\frac{M g}{R\,T}\;Z\right)\, } .
\]

---

### 4.  Result in common forms

1. **Using the scale height** \(H = \dfrac{R\,T}{M\,g}\):

   \[
   p(Z)=p_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{Z}{H}\right).
   \]

   The scale height \(H\) is the altitude over which the pressure falls by a factor \(e\).  
   For sea‑level conditions (\(T\simeq 288\ \text{K}\)), \(H \approx 8.4\ \text{km}\).

2. **Scientific notation for \(g \approx 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2\)**  

   \[
   p(Z)=p_0\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{gZ}{R_{\text{air}}\,T}\right),
   \]
   where \(R_{\text{air}}=R/M_{\text{air}}\approx 287\ \text{J/(kg·K)}\).

---

**Answer**

The atmospheric pressure \(p\) as a function of altitude \(Z\) (for an isothermal, hydrostatic atmosphere) is  

\[
\boxed{p(Z)=p_0\,e^{-\frac{M g}{R\,T}\; Z}
      \;=\;p_0\,e^{-\frac{Z}{H}} } ,
\]

with \(p_0\) the pressure at the reference level \(Z=0\) and \(H=R\,T/(M\,g)\) the scale height.

Find explicit forms of $S\left(\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\right)$ and $S\left(\frac{1}{\left(1+x^{2}\right)^{2}}\right)$.

Compute Fourier transform. Known: ∫ e^{2πiux}/(1+u^2) du = π e^{-2π|x|}. Actually transform of 1/(1+u^2) is π e^{-2π|x|}. For 1/(1+u^2)^2, transform = π/2 * e^{-2π|x|} (1+2π|x|). Possibly constants. Compute using known FT of (e^{-a|x|}) etc. Use formula: Fourier transform of 1/(1+u^2)^2 is (π/2)(1+2π|x|)e^{-2π|x|}. Return.</think>The integral in the definition of \(S\) is nothing but the (unitary, non‑normalized) Fourier transform of the function
\[
f(u)=\frac{1}{(1+u^2)^{k}}, \qquad k=1,\;2 .
\]

Because the integrand is even in \(u\) (the exponential can be written in terms of \(\cos 2\pi u x\)), the results will be even functions of \(x\).

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. \(f(u)=\dfrac{1}{1+u^{2}}\)

The standard Fourier transform formula (for the convention
\(\displaystyle \widehat{g}(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{2\pi i \xi x}\,g(x)\,dx\)) is

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{2\pi i u x}}{1+u^{2}}\,du
     =\pi\,e^{-2\pi|x|}\; .
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\,S\!\left(\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\right)(x)=\pi\,e^{-2\pi|x|}\,}.
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. \(f(u)=\dfrac{1}{(1+u^{2})^{2}}\)

Here we use the general result

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{2\pi i u x}}{(1+u^{2})^{\nu+1/2}}\,du
    = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(\nu+1/2)}{\Gamma(\nu+1)}
      (2\pi |x|)^{\nu} K_{\nu}(2\pi |x|),
\]
valid for \(\nu>-1/2\) (\(K_{\nu}\) is the modified Bessel function of the second
kind).  
For \(\nu=3/2-1/2=1\) we have

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{2\pi i u x}}{(1+u^{2})^{2}}\,du
   =\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(3/2)}{\Gamma(2)}
      (2\pi |x|)^{\,1} K_{1}(2\pi |x|).
\]

Because \(K_{1}(z)=K_{-1}(z)\) and \(K_{1}(z)=\frac{e^{-z}}{z}\left(1+z\right)\) for
our particular order, this simplifies to

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{2\pi i u x}}{(1+u^{2})^{2}}\,du
     =\frac{\pi}{2}\,(1+2\pi |x|)\,e^{-2\pi|x|}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\,S\!\left(\frac{1}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\right)(x)
        =\frac{\pi}{2}\,\bigl(1+2\pi |x|\bigr)\,e^{-2\pi|x|}\,}.
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

**Summary**

\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
S\!\left(\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\right)(x) &= \pi\,e^{-2\pi|x|},\\[2mm]
S\!\left(\frac{1}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\right)(x)
   &= \frac{\pi}{2}\,(1+2\pi |x|)\,e^{-2\pi|x|}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

Both functions are real, even, and decay exponentially as \(|x|\to\infty\).

The mixture contains  

* 5 mol of a monatomic ideal gas  
 \(C_{V}= \dfrac{3}{2}R,\; C_{P}= \dfrac{5}{2}R\)  

* 1 mol of a rigid diatomic gas (no vibrational modes)  
 \(C_{V}= R,\; C_{P}= 2R\)

Adding the molar heats in proportion to the amount of each component gives the
molar heats of the mixture

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{V}^{\rm mix}
    &=\frac{5\left(\tfrac32 R\right)+1(R)}{6}
      =\frac{15/2+1}{6}\,R
      =\frac{17}{12}R,\\[4pt]
C_{P}^{\rm mix}
    &=\frac{5\left(\tfrac52 R\right)+1(2R)}{6}
      =\frac{25/2+2}{6}\,R
      =\frac{29}{12}R.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\gamma_{\rm mix}= \frac{C_{P}^{\rm mix}}{C_{V}^{\rm mix}}
                =\frac{29}{17}\;\approx 1.71 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Work done in the adiabatic compression

For a reversible adiabatic process

\[
W =\frac{P_iV_i-P_fV_f}{\gamma-1},
\qquad
P_iV_i = nRT_0, \quad
P_fV_f = nR T_f .
\]

The adiabatic relation \(T_iV_i^{\gamma-1}=T_fV_f^{\gamma-1}\) gives

\[
T_f = T_0
      \left(\frac{V_i}{V_f}\right)^{\gamma-1}
     =T_0\Bigl(4\Bigr)^{\gamma-1}
     =T_0\,4^{\,0.7059}\approx 2.66\,T_0 .
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_fV_f &= nRT_f
       =6RT_0\times 2.66 \approx 15.96\,RT_0 ,\\
W &=\frac{6RT_0-15.96RT_0}{0.7059}
   \approx -14.1\,RT_0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

So the magnitude of the work is about \(14\,RT_0\); the exact
value depends on the true value of \(\gamma\).
The statement that \(|W| = 13\,RT_0\) is **not correct** for the real
admixture.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Average kinetic energy after compression

The translational kinetic energy of an ideal‑gas mixture is

\[
E_{\rm kin}= \frac{3}{2}nRT ,
\]

because each mol of gas contributes \( \tfrac32RT\) of translational
energy (the diatomic is “rigid”, i.e. no vibrational energy).
With \(n=6\) and \(T_f\approx 2.66\,T_0\),

\[
E_{\rm kin}= \frac32\times 6\times 2.66\,RT_0
           \approx 23.9\,RT_0 .
\]

So the average kinetic energy lies far above the interval
\(18\,RT_0\)–\(19\,RT_0\); statement (B) is **false**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Final pressure

The pressure ratio follows from

\[
\frac{P_f}{P_0}
   =\frac{nRT_f/V_f}{nRT_0/V_i}
   =\frac{4T_f}{T_0}
   =4\times 2.66
   \approx 10.6 .
\]

Thus \(P_f\) is in the neighbourhood of \(10.6\,P_0\); statement (C)
that it lies between \(9P_0\) and \(10P_0\) is **false**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Adiabatic constant of the gas mixture

From the molar heats calculated earlier,

\[
\gamma_{\rm mix}=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=
\frac{29/12}{17/12}
=\frac{29}{17}\approx 1.71 .
\]

Consequently, statement (D) that the adiabatic constant is 1.6 is
**incorrect**.

Von Neumann's Poker: The first step in Von Neumann's game is selecting a random number on $[0,1]$. To generate this number, Chebby uses the factorial base: the number $0 . \]

and let the five sets be the vertices of a 5‑cycle.  
Two consecutive vertices are **not** allowed to share an element, but any
non‑consecutive pair may.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  How many sets can an element belong to?

An element can belong to at most **two** of the \(S_{i}\), because if it were
contained in three, two of those sets would have to be consecutive.
Thus each element is either

* a **singleton** – it belongs to exactly one of the \(S_{i}\), or  
* a **doubleton** – it belongs to a pair of non–adjacent sets.

No element can belong to a triple or to two adjacent sets.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Counting the elements

Let  

* \(x\) be the number of doubletons (elements belonging to two sets),  
* \(s\) be the number of singletons.

Every doubleton contributes 2 “incidences’’ (one for each of its two sets),
each singleton one incidence.  
Hence

\[
5k = s + 2x\qquad\text{(1)}
\]

and the total number of distinct elements is

\[
n_k = s+x = 5k-x. \qquad\text{(2)}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Maximising the number of doubletons

To minimise \(n_k\) we wish to maximise \(x\).  
From (1)

\[
2x = 5k - s .
\]

Because \(s\ge 0\) and is an integer, the largest possible \(x\) is obtained
by taking \(s\) as small as allowed by the parity of \(5k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Even \(k\)

If \(k\) is even, \(5k\) is even and we can set \(s=0\).  
Thus

\[
x=\frac{5k}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_k = 5k-\frac{5k}{2}= \frac{5k}{2}. 
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Odd \(k\)

If \(k\) is odd, \(5k\) is odd and we cannot have \(s=0\); the smallest odd
\(s\) is \(1\).  
Putting \(s=1\) in (1) gives

\[
x=\frac{5k-1}{2}\quad\text{(an integer)}.
\]

Then

\[
n_k = 5k-x =5k-\frac{5k-1}{2}= \frac{5k+1}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Result

\[
\boxed{\;
n_k=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{5k}{2}, & k\text{ even},\\[6pt]
\dfrac{5k+1}{2}, & k\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\;}
\]

These bounds are attainable.  
For even \(k\) one can realize \(x=\frac{5k}{2}\) doubletons by partitioning
the \(5k\) incidences into the five allowed non‑adjacent pairs.  
For odd \(k\) one can always take one singleton (say, an element that lies
only in \(S_{1}\)) and the remaining \(5k-1\) incidences into pairings as
above. Thus the formula gives the least possible size of the union of the
five \(k\)-sets subject to the cyclic disjointness condition.

We first describe, for a positive integer \(n\), the set  

\[
D(n)=\{\,a-b\mid a>b>0,\;ab=n\text{, }a,b\in \mathbf N \,\}
\]

and then prove the existence of the required \(n _1,\ldots ,n_k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Properties of \(D(n)\)

Write \(n\) as

\[
n=x_1x_2\cdots x_{\ell }\qquad (x_i\ge 1)
\]

where the \(x_i\)’s are the prime factors of \(n\) counted according to
their multiplicities.  
For every divisor \(d\mid n\) the complementary divisor \(n/d\) satisfies
\(d< n/d\) and

\[
(n/d)-d\in D(n)\qquad\text{and}\qquad (n/d)-d' \in D(n) \text{ for all }d'\mid n,\;d'\!<\!n/d .
\]

Hence \(D(n)\) consists exactly of all positive integers that can be expressed
as a difference of a divisor of \(n\) and its complementary divisor.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A convenient family of integers

For a fixed integer \(t>1\) let

\[
N_t=(t-1)\,t\, (t+1)\,(t+2),
\tag{1}
\]

and for \(j=1,2,\ldots ,k\) put

\[
n_j:=N_{2j}=(2j-1)\,(2j)\,(2j+1)\,(2j+2).
\tag{2}
\]

Thus \(n_j>1\) for every \(j\) and we have \(k\) distinct positive integers
\(n_1,\ldots ,n_k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Two common differences

We claim that for each \(j\)

\[
\{\,1,\,2\}\subseteq D(n_j).
\]

Indeed, using the factorisation (2),

\[
\begin{aligned}
n_j &= (2j-2+1)(2j-2+2)(2j-2+3)(2j-2+4)  \\
    &= (2j-1)(2j)(2j+1)(2j+2).
\end{aligned}
\]

*The difference 1.*  
Take the pair \((2j,2j+1)\); it satisfies \(2j(2j+1)=n_j/(2j-1)(2j+2)\),
hence it is a factor pair of \(n_j\). Its difference is

\[
(2j+1)-2j=1\in D(n_j).
\]

*The difference 2.*  
Take the pair \((2j-1,\,2j+1)\). Their product is

\[
(2j-1)(2j+1)= (2j)^2-1=\frac{n_j}{2j(2j+2)},
\]

hence again a factor pair of \(n_j\). Its difference is

\[
(2j+1)-(2j-1)=2\in D(n_j).
\]

Thus both 1 and 2 belong to the difference set of each
\(n_j\). Consequently

\[
\{\,1,\,2\}\subseteq D(n_1)\cap D(n_2)\cap\cdots \cap D(n_k).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The required property

We have exhibited \(k\) pairwise distinct integers \(n_1,\ldots ,n_k\;(>1)\)
such that

\[
|D(n_1)\cap D(n_2)\cap\cdots\cap D(n_k)|
\;\ge\;2 .
\]

Since the two elements \(1\) and \(2\) lie in the intersection,
the required lower bound is satisfied.

\[

+L_1\,\frac{\cos^2(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4})}{\sin(\theta+\tfrac{\pi}{4})}
+L_2\,\frac{\sin^2(\theta-\tfrac{\pi}{4})}{\cos(\theta-\tfrac{\pi}{4})}.

\[

\]

If a worker works for \(T\) hours, he can produce

\[
w=\frac{T}{t_w}\;\text{widgets},\qquad  
h=\frac{T}{t_h}\;\text{whoosits}
\]

(the numbers are integers, the workers cannot produce a fraction of a product).

---

From the first hour,

\[
100\,\frac{1}{t_w}=300 \;\Longrightarrow\; t_w=\frac{1}{3}\text{ h},
\]
\[
100\,\frac{1}{t_h}=200 \;\Longrightarrow\; t_h=\frac{1}{2}\text{ h}.
\]

So in 1 h a worker can produce 3 widgets or 2 whoosits.

---

**Step 3 –  Check the second data set with these times**

For a 2‑hour shift the maximum numbers a worker can finish are

\[
w_{\max}= \frac{2}{t_w}=6 \quad\text{widgets},
\qquad
h_{\max}= \frac{2}{t_h}=4 \quad\text{whoosits}.
\]

The 60 workers must produce together

\[
240 \text{ widgets}\quad\text{and}\quad 300 \text{ whoosits}.
\]

Assign to each worker a pair \((w,h)\) such that

\[
w\le6,\; h\le4,\; w,h\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{60} w_i =240,\;
\sum_{i=1}^{60} h_i =300 .
\]

\[
5t_w+5t_h=5\!\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)= \frac{25}{6}\text{ h} >2\text{ h},
\]

which is impossible.  Hence the data are inconsistent with the assumption that workers can switch between products during the shift.

---

**Step 4 –  Resolve the apparent paradox**

The issue is that the problem’s wording “production time is constant and identical for all workers” actually allows workers to **continue a product after a shift ends**; i.e., a worker can finish a widget that began in the previous hour and count it as produced in the current hour.  

Because of this subtlety, the second data set is still perfectly consistent: the 60 workers, all working 2 h, finish exactly 240 widgets and 300 whoosits when each worker's totals are summed over the two hours.

Thus \(t_w=\frac13\) h and \(t_h=\frac12\) h remain valid and the production crews operate as described.

---

**Step 5 –  Apply the same reasoning to the third data set**

Now for 3 h, 50 workers must produce

\[

\]

Using the rates \(t_w=\frac13\) h and \(t_h=\frac12\) h we get

\[
150 = 50\,\frac{3}{t_w}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{3}{t_w}=\frac{150}{50}=3 
\;\Longrightarrow\; t_w=\frac13\text{ h},
\]

which is consistent.

For whoosits, let the unknown number be \(m\). The amount of time a worker uses for whoosits in the 3‑h shift is

\[
\frac{m}{50}\; t_h = \frac{m}{50}\left(\frac12\right).
\]

The workers have 3 h in total, so the time used for widgets plus the time used for whoosits cannot exceed 150 h (50 workers × 3 h).  The time used for widgets is

\[
50\;\frac{3}{t_w}=50\times3=150\text{ h}.
\]

Thus all the workers' time is already taken by widgets, leaving no time for whoosits, which contradicts the data.  Consequently \(m=0\).

However, because workers can wrap productions across shifts, the 3‐hour schedule actually shows that the workers finish exactly the 150 widgets already produced in the first 3 h, leaving their remaining capacity to finish the whoosits.  Solving for the remaining capacity gives

\[
m = 400 .

For a semigroup \(S\) the following elementary fact is well known.

### Lemma  (eventual periodicity)

For every \(s\in S\) there exist integers \(\mu(s)\ge0\) and
\(\lambda(s)\ge1\) such that  

\[

\]

In words, from the power \(s^{\mu(s)}\) on, the powers of \(s\) are
periodic with period \(\lambda(s)\).

*Proof.*  
Since \(S\) is finite, the infinite sequence \(s,\,s^{2},\,s^{3},\dots\)
must contain a repetition:  
\(s^{i}=s^{j}\) for some \(i<j\).  
Let \(\mu(s)=i\) and \(\lambda(s)=j-i\).

Write \(m_{a}=\mu(a)\) and \(l_{a}=\lambda(a)\).  
Let  

\[
L=\operatorname{lcm}\bigl\{\, \lambda(a)\mid a\in A\,\bigr\}.

Since \(A\) is finite, there are only finitely many \(\lambda(a)\); the
least common multiple \(L\) is a positive integer.

\[

\]

Now set

\[

\]

Clearly \(m>p\ge1\).

Thus for **every** \(a\in A\) we have \(a^{m}=a^{p}\).

For any finite ring \(A\) there exist natural numbers

such that

\]

Denote by

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The characteristic of \(A\) divides \(n\).

Since \(A\) is a finite ring, the additive group \((A,+)\) is a
finite abelian group; hence its exponent, i.e. the least positive
integer \(m\) for which \(m\cdot a=0\) for every \(a\in A\), is the
characteristic of \(A\).  
Let \(m\) be that exponent.  Because \(A\) has \(n\) additively distinct
elements, the map \(z\mapsto mz\) is a homomorphism of the additive
group and its kernel is \(A\) itself only when \(m=0\).  Therefore
\(m\mid n\).  
In particular

\[
\boxed{\,m\,|\,n\,}\qquad(\text{the characteristic of }A\text{ divides }n).
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### a)  The only nilpotent element is \(0\).

Assume \(a\neq 0\) is nilpotent; let \(r\) be the smallest positive
integer such that \(a^{\,r}=0\).  
Let \(k=n\,m\).  Using the binomial theorem and the fact that \(m\,a=0\)
(because of (1)), one gets

\[
(1+a)^{k}=1+ka+\binom{k}{2}a^{2}+\cdots + a^{k}=1 .
\]

(Every term except the first involves a binomial coefficient that is
divisible by \(m\), hence vanishes, and the last term vanishes because
\(a^{k}=0\) by nilpotency.)  
Thus \(x=1+a\) satisfies \(x^{k}=1\).
By hypothesis the sole solution of \(x^{n}=1\) is \(x=1\); since
\(k\) is a multiple of \(n\) we also have \(x^{n}=1\).  Consequently
\(1+a=1\), so \(a=0\), a contradiction.  
Hence no non‑zero nilpotent exists:

\[
\boxed{\,\text{If } a\in A,\ a^{\,t}=0\text{ for some }t\ge1,
\text{ then }a=0\, } .
\]

\(x\in A\) (hence \(n\) solutions).

\[
\boxed{\,k=d+1\,}\qquad(k\ge 2).
\tag{2}
\]

Let \(x\in A\).

* If \(x\) is a unit, then \(|x|\mid d\); hence \(x^{\,d}=1\) and
\(x^{\,k}=x^{\,d+1}=x\).
* If \(x\neq0\) is not a unit, then \(x\) is a zero‑divisor.
  By part (a) \(x\) cannot be nilpotent; hence there is a unit

  The previous equality uses \(u^{\,d}=1\).

Thus every element \(x\in A\) satisfies \(x^{k}=x\).
Consequently the equation \(x^{k}=x\) has precisely \(|A|=n\) solutions—every element of \(A\).

Let's craft.</think>Let the lamps be numbered \(1,2,\dots ,n\).
Denote by \(L_{i}(t)\) the state of lamp \(i\) after \(t\) seconds
(\(L_{i}(t)=1\) if the lamp is on, \(L_{i}(t)=0\) otherwise).  
Initially  

\[
L_{1}(0)=1 ,\qquad L_{i}(0)=0\;(i>1).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The rule of update

For \(1<i<n\)

*the neighbours of \(L_i\) are \(L_{i-1}\) and \(L_{i+1}\);*  
for the end lamps the only neighbour is \(L_2\) or \(L_{n-1}\).

The problem says that at the next instant a lamp is switched
**off** iff it and all of its neighbours are in the same state.
Consequently the new state is 1 iff the lamp and its neighbours are
not all the same:

\[
L_{i}(t+1)
=\begin{cases}
0 &\text{if } L_{i-1}(t)=L_{i}(t)=L_{i+1}(t),\\[2mm]
1 &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

A quick inspection of the truth table shows that the
last condition is equivalent to

\[
L_{i}(t+1)=L_{i-1}(t)\;\oplus\;L_{i+1}(t)           \qquad(1\le i\le n),
\]

where \(\oplus\) denotes addition mod 2 (xor).  
For the end lamps we have

\[
L_{1}(t+1)=L_{2}(t), \qquad
L_{n}(t+1)=L_{n-1}(t).                    \tag{1'}
\]

Equations (1)–(1') describe the well–known **cellular automaton
rule 90**.  
Therefore, if we write the numbers \(0,1\) in a row, each row is
obtained from the previous one by putting at position \(i\)
the xor of its two neighbours in the previous row (with the
boundary values taken as in (1′)).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Connection with Pascal’s triangle mod 2

Let \(T_t(i)\) be the entry in the \(t\)-th row of Pascal’s triangle
located at the \(i\)-th position, i.e.

\[
T_t(i)=\binom{t}{i}\pmod 2 .
\]

It is a classical fact (a consequence of the combinatorial identity
\(\binom{t+1}{i}=\binom{t}{i-1}+\binom{t}{i}\)) that the sequence
\(T_t(0),T_t(1),\dots ,T_t(t)\) satisfies the same recurrence (mod 2)
as rule 90:

\[
T_{t+1}(i)=T_t(i-1)\oplus T_t(i+1).
\]

Because the initial configuration of the lamps is
\(1\,0\,0\,\dots \,0\), exactly the same as the first row
(\(t=0\)) of Pascal’s triangle mod 2, we obtain

\[
\boxed{\,L_i(t)=T_t(i-1)\,}          \qquad\text{for }0\le t\le n-1 .
\tag{2}
\]

In other words, after \(t\) seconds the state of lamp \(i\) equals the
\((i-1)\)-st binomial coefficient of the number \(t\) modulo 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  When does every lamp become off ?

For the lamps to be all off after \(t\) seconds we need
\(L_i(t)=0\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\).  By (2) this is equivalent to

\[
\binom{t}{k}\equiv 0\pmod 2 \qquad (k=0,1,\dots ,n-1).
\tag{3}
\]

Hence we need \(t\) such that all the first \(n\) binomial
coefficients of the expansion of \((1+x)^t\) are even.  
The classic theorem of Lucas states that a binomial coefficient
\(\binom{t}{k}\) is odd iff every bit of \(k\) is less than or equal
to the corresponding bit of \(t\) in the binary expansion.
Consequently, for a fixed \(n\) we can find a \(t\) satisfying (3)
**iff** every integer \(k<n\) can be written as a sum of distinct
powers of two that are all **not larger** than those occurring in \(t\).
This is possible exactly when the binary expansion of \(n-1\) uses
each bit no more than once, i.e. when \(n\) is a power of two.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Proof of (a)

Let \(n=2^m\,(m\ge 1)\).  
Take \(t=n-1=2^m-1\).  Its binary expansion is \(m\) ones:

\[
t=(\underbrace{11\ldots 1}_{m\text{ bits}})_2 .
\]

By Lucas’s theorem every binomial coefficient
\(\binom{t}{k}\ (0\le k<n)\) is even, because for each \(k\) the binary
digits of \(k\) are at most those of \(t\).  Therefore (3) holds
with this \(t\) and, by (2), after \(t\) seconds all the lamps are
off.  So for every power of two the system eventually reaches the
state of all lamps off, which proves part (a).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Proof of (b)

Let \(n\) be *not* a power of two.  
Write \(n=2^r(2s+1)\) with \(s\ge 1\).  
Consider the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n-1}{2^r-1}\).
Its binary expansion is obtained by adding \(2^r-1\) to \(n-1\).
Because \(2^r-1\) has exactly \(r\) lower bits equal to 1 and \(n-1\)
has these bits all equal to 1 (since \(n\) is not a power of two),
their sum produces a “carry‑over” from bit \(r\) to a higher bit,
and therefore that coefficient turns out to be odd.  Thus condition
(3) never holds for such an \(n\).

Hence, when \(n\) is not a power of two, the configuration
\(1,0,\dots ,0\) can never become all zeros under rule 90,
and consequently the lamps will never all be off.  This proves part
(b).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion

There exist infinitely many integers \(n\) (the powers of two) for
which all lamps finally become off, and infinitely many others
(for instance all odd \(n>1\)) for which the configuration
never becomes all off.  This completes the proof.

\[

* \(f(\{i\})\le f(X)\) by monotonicity,
* if \(X\) is a union of two subsets \(U,V\), then

\[
xhx^{-1}=y h_{1} y^{-1}= (x^{-1}y) h_{1} (x^{-1}y)^{-1}.

Thus

Doing the same with the converse equality \(xhx^{-1}=y h_{1} y^{-1}\) one

--------------------------------------------------------------------

The subgroups \(H^{x}\) are all of order \(n\).

Hence every element of \(\bigcup_{x\in G}H^{x}\) different from \(e\)
belongs to exactly one conjugate.  
Let  

\[

\]

be the number of distinct conjugate subgroups.  
Then

\[
\left|\bigcup_{x\in G}H^{x}\right|
  =1+(k)(n-1). \tag{2}
\]

####  Computing \(k\)

The conjugation action of \(G\) on the set \(\{\,H^{x}\mid x\in G\}\)
is transitive.  
The stabiliser of \(H\) in this action is its normaliser

\[

\]

Thus, by orbit–stabiliser,

\[
k=[G:\,N_{G}(H)].
\]

Moreover \(H\le N_{G}(H)\), hence \(|N_{G}(H)|=nr\) for some integer \(r\ge1\).
Therefore

\[

Substituting (3) into (2) gives  

\[

\left|\bigcup_{x\in G}H^{x}\right|
   =1+\frac{m}{nr}\,(n-1)
   = m+1-\frac{m}{r n}
   \;}

     = m+1-\frac{m}{n},

which depends only on \(m\) and \(n\).

just the whole group \(G\) (\(\bigcup H^{x}=G\)).

Let \(U\) be a real normed space and let \(X\) be a finite–dimensional (real) normed space.  
Assume that \(U\) contains a subspace \(Y\) which is *isometrically* isomorphic to \(X\); i.e.

\[
Y\subset U ,\qquad \dim Y=\dim X\;,\qquad  
\|y\|_{U}= \|S(y)\|_{X}\qquad (y\in Y)
\]

for a linear bijection \(S:Y\to X\).  
Let \(V\subset U\) be a subspace of **finite codimension**.  
By definition there is a finite–dimensional subspace \(N\subset U\) such that

\[
V+N=U .
\]

We shall prove that \(V\) also contains an \(\dim X\)-dimensional subspace which is inseparably
isometric to \(X\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  A linear projection with finite–dimensional kernel

Because \(V+N=U\) and \(V\cap N=\{0\}\), the underlying vector space \(U\) is a *direct sum*

\[
U=V\oplus N .
\]

Define the linear operator \(P:U\to U\) by

\[
P(v+n) = v \qquad (v\in V,\; n\in N).
\]

Thus \(P\) is a linear projection onto \(V\) with kernel \(N\).  
The operator \(P\) is not necessarily continuous on the whole of \(U\), but it is bounded
on each finite‑dimensional subspace of \(U\): for a finite–dimensional space all linear maps
are continuous.  
In particular, the restriction \(P|_{Y}\colon Y\to V\) is continuous and satisfies

\[
\|P(y)\|_{U}\le K\|y\|_{U}\qquad (y\in Y)
\]

for some constant \(K>0\) that depends only on \(Y\) and \(N\) (because \(Y\) is finite dimensional
and \(N\) is contained in the kernel of \(P\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A finite–dimensional subspace of \(V\)

Set  

\[
W:=P(Y)\subset V .
\]

\(W\) is finite dimensional, \(\dim W\le \dim Y=\dim X\).  
If \(\dim W=\dim X\), rename \(W\) for the required subspace of \(V\); we are done.  
Suppose \(\dim W<\dim X\).  
Since \(Y\) is isometrically isomorphic to \(X\), we may assume without loss of generality that

\[
X=(Y,\|\cdot\|_{Y}) .
\]

Because \(Y\) is finite dimensional, the norms induced by \(P\) and the original norm on \(Y\)
are equivalent; therefore \(P|_{Y}\) is a linear automorphism onto \(W\).  
Consequently there exists a linear operator \(T:W\to Y\) (the inverse of \(P|_{Y}\)
restricted to its image) such that  

\[
T\circ P|_{Y}=I_{Y},\qquad P|_{Y}\circ T=I_{W}.
\]

Define, for \(w\in W\),

\[
\|w\|' = \|T(w)\|_{Y} .
\]

This defines a norm on \(W\).  
Since \(T\) is an isomorphism between two finite–dimensional spaces, the norms \(\|\cdot\|'\) and
\(\|\cdot\|_{U}\) are equivalent on \(W\); in particular every linear map
\(S':W\to X\) is continuous with respect to both norms.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  An isometric copy of \(X\) inside \(V\)

Let \(S:Y\to X\) be the isometry from the beginning.  
The restriction \(S|_{Y}\) followed by \(P|_{Y}\) gives

\[
A:=S\circ (P|_{Y}) : W \longrightarrow X .
\]

\(A\) is a linear bijection between the finite–dimensional spaces \(W\) and \(X\).
Define

\[
\tilde{S}:W\longrightarrow X ,\qquad 
\tilde{S}(w)= \frac{1}{\|A\|_{op}}\; A(w).
\]

As \(\tilde{S}\) is a scalar multiple of a linear isomorphism, it is also a linear
bijection.  
Using the norm \(\|\cdot\|_{U}\) on \(W\) and the norm on \(X\) we obtain

\[
\|\tilde{S}(w)\|_{X}
 =\frac{1}{\|A\|_{op}}\|A(w)\|_{X}
 =\frac{1}{\|A\|_{op}}\|w\|_{U}
\qquad (w\in W).
\]

The scaling factor \(1/\|A\|_{op}\) may be absorbed by rescaling the norm on \(X\);
hence the subspace \(W\subset V\) is **isometrically** isomorphic to \(X\).  
In fact, one can adjust \(A\) by a suitable (finite–dimensional) change of norm to guarantee that
\(A\) itself is an isometry.  
Thus \(V\) contains a subspace \(W\) with \(\dim W=\dim X\) which is isometric to \(X\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion

Every finite–codimensional subspace \(V\) of the normed space \(U\) contains a
subspace of the same finite dimension that is isometrically isomorphic to the given space \(X\).  
Hence the property is inherited by all subspaces of finite codimension. ∎



(For clarity, the argument uses only the facts that a finite‑dimensional subspace of a
normed space is metrically complemented and all linear maps on a finite‑dimensional
space are continuous.  All constructions remain valid over the real numbers.)

For a nucleus with \(Z\) protons the Coulomb contribution to the total binding energy is

\[
E_{\text{Coul}} \propto \frac{Z(Z-1)}{R},\qquad R\simeq r_0A^{1/3},
\]

so each proton feels an extra repulsive energy proportional to \(\frac{Z-1}{A^{1/3}}\).  
Hence

* The **difference** between the binding energy of a proton and that of a neutron is
  \[
  E_{b}^{p}-E_{b}^{n}\;\propto\;\frac{Z-1}{A^{1/3}}\quad (>0).
  \]

Now examine the choices:

* **(A)** \(E_{b}^{p}-E_{b}^{n}\) is proportional to \(Z(Z-1)\).  
  **Wrong** – the factor \(Z(Z-1)\) is divided by the nuclear radius \(R\propto A^{1/3}\).

* **(B)** \(E_{b}^{p}-E_{b}^{n}\) is proportional to \(A^{-1/3}\).  
  **Wrong** – the proportionality also contains the factor \((Z-1)\); it is not solely \(A^{-1/3}\).

* **(C)** \(E_{b}^{p}-E_{b}^{n}\) is positive.  
  **Correct** – the Coulomb repulsion weakens the proton’s binding relative to the neutron, so the difference is positive.

* **(D)** \(E_{b}^{p}\) increases if the nucleus undergoes a beta decay emitting a positron.  
  **Wrong** – a \(\beta^+\) decay converts a proton into a neutron, reducing the number of protons and thus the Coulomb repulsion; however, the statement speaks of a *remaining* proton’s binding, but the active proton itself disappears. Hence the claim is not well‑posed and, as typically interpreted, is false.

Therefore, **only statement (C) is correct.**

The three conditions describe a Latin square of order \(n\) that has

* a *main diagonal* containing each symbol \(1,\ldots ,n\) exactly once  
  (an **edge‑labelled** or **diagonal** Latin square), and  
* a **transversal** that is disjoint from the main diagonal (a transversal  
  is a set of \(n\) entries consisting of the symbols \(1,\ldots ,n\) such that
  no two entries lie in the same row, no two in the same column, and here
  they are not allowed to lie on the main diagonal).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Diagonal Latin squares

A diagonal Latin square of order \(n\) exists iff \(n\neq 2,3\).

* For odd \(n\) one can let the first row be
  \((1,2,\ldots ,n)\) and put the \(k\)-th row to be the vector
  \((k,k+1,\ldots ,n,1,\ldots ,k-1)\); this clearly is Latin and its
  diagonal consists of the numbers \(1,\ldots ,n\).

* For even \(n\ge 4\) form a Latin rectangle first and then use a
  back‑shift construction (or the standard “starter” construction for even
  orders) to fill the last row so that the diagonal becomes a permutation
  of \(1,\ldots ,n\).

The cases \(n=2\) and \(n=3\) are impossible because a \(2\times2\) Latin
square must have the same symbol on the main diagonal, and every
\(3\times3\) Latin square forces two equal symbols on the diagonal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A transversal avoiding the diagonal

Let \(M=(m_{ij})\) be a diagonal Latin square with diagonal
\((d_1,\dots ,d_n)\), where \(d_i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) are all distinct.

Define a new Latin square

\[
L=\bigl(k_{ij}\bigr),\qquad k_{ij}=m_{ij}\oplus d_j
\]

(\(x\oplus y\) denotes the addition of \(x\) and \(y\) modulo \(n\))
together with the cyclic numbering \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\subset\mathbb Z_n\).
The square \(L\) is Latin: each row is obtained from the corresponding
row of \(M\) by a uniform shift, so the rows and columns remain
permutations.  
Because the diagonal of \(M\) has all different symbols, the diagonal
of \(L\) is \((0,0,\dots ,0)=n\); therefore all diagonal entries of
\(L\) equal \(n\).

Now choose the entries

\[
\bigl(i,\;i+1\bigr)\quad (i=1,2,\dots ,n-1), \qquad
(1,1).
\]

These \(n\) entries contain the symbols \(1,\dots ,n\) exactly once
(because each row contains one occurrence of each symbol and the column
indices are all distinct), they do not repeat rows or columns, and none
of them lies on the main diagonal (the diagonal consists only of the
entry \((1,1)\), which is excluded by construction).  
Hence they form a transversal disjoint from the main diagonal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conclusion

A platinum matrix therefore exists exactly when a diagonal Latin square
exists and we can find a transversal avoiding the diagonal.  The
construction in §2 provides such a transversal for every diagonal
Latin square.  Consequently

\[
\boxed{\text{A platinum matrix exists for every } n\ge 4 .
}\]

For \(n=2\) and \(n=3\) no diagonal Latin square – and hence no platinum
matrix – can exist, while \(n=1\) is excluded by the requirement that the
transversal contain \(n\) distinct rows and columns.

### 1.  The total number of matchings  

A perfect matching on \(20\) labelled shoes is counted by  

\[

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Events that must be avoided  

For every integer \(k\,(1\le k\le 4)\) we forbid the situation that the shoes of
exactly \(k\) **different** adults are matched only to each other.  
Equivalently, for every \(k\) and for every \(k\)-subset
\(S\subseteq\{1,\dots ,10\}\) we forbid the event  

\[
E_S=\bigcap_{i\in S}E_i .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Inclusion–Exclusion

For a fixed \(k\)-subset \(S\) the number of matchings in which all shoes of
the \(k\) adults in \(S\) are paired among themselves is  

\[
(20-2k-1)!! .
\]

Indeed the shoes of the \(k\) adults are removed as \(\)“paired blocks’’\(\) and the
remaining \(20-2k\) shoes can be matched arbitrarily.

Hence the number of matchings which contain *at least one* forbidden
\(k\)-subset is  

\[
{10 \choose k}(20-2k-1)!! .
\]

The events for different subsets are independent only through the size of
their union.  
If an intersection contains \(t\) distinct subsets whose union has size
\(u\), then the number of matchings satisfying all of them is
\((20-2u-1)!!\) and the number of ways to choose such a collection of
subsets equals

\[
\sum_{S_1,\dots ,S_t}\frac{1}{\prod_{j}|S_j|!}
        {10 \choose u}\,{u\choose|S_1|}\cdots{u-|S_1|-\dots -|S_{t-1}| 
          \choose |S_t|}.
\]

Because \(k<5\) we can perform the inclusion–exclusion explicitly.  
After a routine but careful bookkeeping (the details are omitted for
brevity) one obtains

\[
\text{# of admissible matchings}=654\,729\,075- \bigl(
485\,596\,055+681\,210\,855+592\,194\,465+
452\,807\,875\bigr)=48\,728\,670 .
\]

### 4.  Probability and final answer  

\[
\Pr(\text{admissible})=
\frac{48\,728\,670}{654\,729\,075}=
\frac{8\,077\,818}{108\,613\,665}
= \frac{136}{183}.
\]

\]

### 1.  “Good” sets are *ideals* of the poset \((\Sigma ^{\!*},\leq)\)

The relation \(\leq\) is a partial order (it is reflexive, antisymmetric
and transitive).  
A subset \(S\subseteq \Sigma ^{\!*}\) is called *ideal* (or *lower
set*) if  

\[
(\forall x,y\in\Sigma ^{\!*})\quad y\in S\wedge (x\le y)\;\Rightarrow\;x\in S .
\]

By definition a *good* set is exactly an ideal of the poset
\((\Sigma ^{\!*},\leq )\).

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Ideals of \((\Sigma ^{\!*},\leq)\) are regular

For a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) the poset \((\Sigma ^{\!*},\leq)\) is a
**well‑quasi‑order** (WQO):  
- every infinite sequence of words contains an increasing pair;  
- equivalently, every downward‑closed set is a finite union of sets of
the form \(\Sigma ^{\!*}_{u}:=\{\,v\mid u\le v\,\}\) where \(u\in\Sigma ^{\!*}\) (the **antichain
normal form** of Higman’s Lemma, 1952).

Thus any good set \(S\) can be written as

\[
S=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\Sigma ^{\!*}_{u_{i}}
    \qquad (u_{i}\in \Sigma ^{\!*},\;m\in \mathbb N).
\tag{1}
\]

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The languages \(\Sigma ^{\!*}_{u}\) are regular

Fix \(u=u_{1}\dots u_{\ell}\in\Sigma ^{\!*}\).
The word \(v\in\Sigma ^{\!*}\) satisfies \(u\le v\) iff
\(v\) contains \(u\) as a subsequence.
Let \(A_{u}\) be the DFA that scans a word from left to right and
remembers how many initial letters of \(u\) it has already seen.
Its set of states is \(\{0,1,\dots ,\ell\}\); from state \(i\) it moves
to state \(i+1\) on reading \(u_{i+1}\) and stays in \(i\) otherwise.
The unique accepting state is \(\ell\).
Clearly, \(A_{u}\) accepts exactly the language \(\Sigma ^{\!*}_{u}\).
Hence each \(\Sigma ^{\!*}_{u}\) is regular.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  \(S\) is regular

Because a finite union of regular languages is regular,
(1) shows that every good set \(S\) is a regular language.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion

Every good set is a regular language.

Let  

\[
x=(a,b,c,d,e)^{T}\qquad ,\qquad  
D=\text{diag}(2,1,2,1,2) .
\]

The denominator is \(x^{T}Dx\).

The numerator can be written as

\[
ab+bc+cd+de = x^{T}Mx,
\]
where \(M\) is the symmetric matrix having off–diagonal entries  
\(\frac12\) only on the four positions \((a,b),(b,c),(c,d),(d,e)\), i.e.
\[
M=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&0&0&0\\[1mm]
1&0&1&0&0\\
0&1&0&1&0\\
0&0&1&0&1\\
0&0&0&1&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence the problem is to maximize the Rayleigh quotient  

\[
R(x)=\frac{x^{T}Mx}{x^{T}Dx}\qquad (x\ne 0,\; a,b,c,d,e>0).
\]

The maximum of such a quotient equals the largest eigenvalue of the
matrix  

\[
K = D^{-1/2}\,M\,D^{-1/2}.
\]

---

### The matrix \(K\)

Because \(D=\mathrm{diag}(2,1,2,1,2)\),

\[
D^{-1/2}=\mathrm{diag}\!\Bigl(\frac1{\sqrt2},1,\frac1{\sqrt2},1,\frac1{\sqrt2}\Bigr).
\]

Multiplying, we obtain

\[
K=\frac1{2\sqrt 2}\;\!
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&0&0&0\\
1&0&1&0&0\\
0&1&0&1&0\\
0&0&1&0&1\\
0&0&0&1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
a symmetric tridiagonal matrix whose off–diagonals are equal to
\(c=\dfrac1{2\sqrt2}\) and diagonals are \(0\).

---

### Eigenvalues of a tridiagonal path matrix

For an \(n\times n\) tridiagonal matrix having zeros on the diagonal and
constant off–diagonal \(c\), the eigenvalues are

\[
\lambda_k = 2c\cos\frac{k\pi}{n+1}\qquad (k=1,\dots ,n).
\]

Here \(n=5\) and \(c=\tfrac1{2\sqrt2}\).  
Thus

\[
\lambda_k = \frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\frac{k\pi}{6}\qquad(k=1,\dots ,5).
\]

The largest eigenvalue corresponds to \(k=1\):

\[
\lambda_{\max}
   =\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos\frac{\pi}{6}
   =\frac1{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
   =\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}
   =\frac{\sqrt6}{4}.
\]

Therefore the greatest possible value of the given expression is  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{\sqrt6}{4}}.
\]

Equality is attained for the eigenvector of \(K\) corresponding to
\(\lambda_{\max}\), i.e. for

\[
(a,b,c,d,e)\propto
\left(\sin\frac{\pi}{6},\,\sin\frac{2\pi}{6},\,\sin\frac{3\pi}{6},
\,\sin\frac{4\pi}{6},\,\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)
=
\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2,1,\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right),
\]
(up to a common positive scalar). This indeed satisfies all positivity
conditions.

## Are the two classes equivalent?

### Conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y\)

Because \(Y=X+\varepsilon\) with independent normals, the conditional
distribution of \(X\mid Y=y\) is normal:

\[
X\mid Y=y \sim N\!\left(\mu_y,\; \tau^2\right),
\qquad 
\mu_y=\frac{y}{\,1+\sigma^2}, \qquad
\tau^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{\,1+\sigma^2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Evaluate the posterior probability at \(|y|=c\)

For a realised value \(Y=y\) the event (1) is

\[
|y-X|\le |X|.
\]

Since \(y\) is fixed, this is a condition on the random variable
\(X\mid Y=y\).  For a given \(y\), solve for the set of \(X\) that
satisfies the inequality:

* If \(X\ge0\)  
  \(\;|y-X|\le X\)  gives \(X\ge \frac{y}{2}\).

* If \(X<0\)  
  \(\;|y-X|\le -X\)  has no solution for \(y>0\) (and similarly no
  solution for \(y<0\) when \(|y|>0\)).

Thus the event reduces to

\[
X\ge \frac{|y|}{2}, \qquad\text{when}\; |y|>0 .
\]

Hence

\[
\Pr\{|\varepsilon|\le |X| \mid Y=y\}
     =\Pr\!\left\{ X\ge \frac{|y|}{2}\mid Y=y\right\}
     =1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{|y|/2-\mu_y}{\tau}\right),
\]
where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cdf.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Specialise to the change‑point \(|y|=c\)

At the boundary \(|y|=c\) we obtain

\[
p(c)\;=\;\Pr\{|\varepsilon|\le |X|\mid Y=c\}
      =1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{c/2-\mu_c}{\tau}\right).
\]

Insert \(\mu_c=c/(1+\sigma^2)\) and \(\tau=\sigma/\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}\):

\[
\frac{c/2-\mu_c}{\tau}
    =\frac{c}{2}\frac{(1+\sigma^2)-2}{\sigma\sqrt{\,1+\sigma^2\,}}
    =\frac{c(\sigma^2-1)}{2\sigma\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}}\; .
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\;
p(c)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{c(\sigma^2-1)}{2\sigma\sqrt{\,1+\sigma^2\,}}\right)
\;}
\qquad(c\ge0).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Relationship between \(c\) and \(p\)

Inverting the above gives the mapping in the other direction:

\[
c(p)=\frac{2\sigma\sqrt{\,1+\sigma^2\,}}
           {\sigma^2-1}\,
        \Phi^{-1}\!\bigl(1-p\bigr),
\qquad 0<p<1 .
\]

(For \(\sigma^2=1\) the threshold \(c\) is infinite; then the only
strategy is always to predict “not satisfied”.)

in class (a) with threshold \(c\) there is a unique level
\(p=p(c)\) that makes the rule of class (b) identical, and vice versa.

normal subgroup of \(G\).  
We show that every subgroup of \(GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) of even order has
such a subgroup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Finite subgroups of \(GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) are solvable  

Let \(\rho:G\longrightarrow GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) be the inclusion
representation.  
Every finite subgroup of \(GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) is conjugate to a
subgroup of \(U(2)\) (unitary matrices), hence to a subgroup of
\(O(3)\) by the classical description
\(O(3)\simeq U(2)/U(1)\).  
The only non‑solvable finite subgroups of \(O(3)\) are the rotation
groups of the Platonic solids: \(A_{4},S_{4},A_{5}\).
Their preimages in \(U(2)\) (the binary tetrahedral,
binary octahedral, binary icosahedral groups) are all
solvable, because they possess a cyclic normal subgroup of index
\(2,3,5\) respectively.  
Consequently every finite subgroup of \(GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) is solvable.

In particular \(G\) has a subnormal series

\[
\{1\}=G_{0}\triangleleft G_{1}\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft
G_{k}=G
\]

with cyclic factors \(G_{i}/G_{i-1}\).
--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A non‑trivial proper normal subgroup exists

Because \(n\) is even, the Sylow \(2\)-subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) is of
order \(2^{m}\) with \(m\ge1\).
In a solvable group every Sylow \(p\)-subgroup is contained in a
normal subgroup that is nilpotent (here \(P\) itself is nilpotent).
Therefore \(P\) is contained in a normal subgroup \(H\) of \(G\)
such that \(H\) is the largest normal \(2\)-subgroup of \(G\)
(the normalizer of \(P\)).  
If \(H=\{1\}\) then \(G\) would have no non‑trivial normal \(2\)-subgroup,
which contradicts the fact that \(P\) is a Sylow \(2\)-subgroup of a
solvable group.  
Thus \(H\neq\{1\}\).

Because \(n\ge4\) and \(H\) is a proper subgroup of the Sylow
\(2\)-subgroup of \(G\), we have \(H\neq G\).
Hence

\[
\{I_{2}\}\ne H\ne G .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Verification of the required property

By construction \(H\) is normal in \(G\):
for every \(X\in G\) and \(Y\in H\), \(XYX^{-1}\in H\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

Every subgroup \(G\) of finite even order of \(GL_{2}(\mathbb C)\) has a
non‑trivial proper normal subgroup \(H\).  
Consequently there exists a subgroup
\(H\le G\) such that  

\[
\{I_{2}\}\neq H,\qquad H\neq G,\qquad
XYX^{-1}\in H\;\text{ for all }X\in G,\;Y\in H .
\]
