A number \(m\) is called **fine** if there is a prime \(p\) such that  
\(p\mid m\) and \(p^{2}\nmid m\).
If no such prime exists then every prime factor of \(m\) occurs at least twice:
\(m\) is a *square‑ful* number (a perfect square times a square‑free part
with all exponents \( \ge 2\)).  
Thus the set of non‑fine numbers consists exactly of the square‑ful integers
in \([n]\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Bounding the number of square‑ful integers up to \(N\)

Let  

\[
Q_k=\{\,m\le N : \exists\,p \text{ prime with } p^k\mid m\,\},
\qquad k\ge 2 .
\]

A number is square‑ful iff it belongs to \(\bigcup_{k\ge 2} Q_k\).
For a fixed \(k\) every member of \(Q_k\) is a multiple of some \(p^k\),
so \(|Q_k|\le\lfloor N/p^k\rfloor\).
Summing over all primes,

\[
|Q_k|\le \sum_{p\le N^{1/k}}\Big\lfloor\frac{N}{p^k}\Big\rfloor
       \le N\sum_{p\le N^{1/k}}\frac1{p^k}
       \le N\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac1{n^k}.
\]

The tail \( \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} n^{-k} \) is dominated by the first term  
\(1/2^{\,k}\), so

\[
|Q_k|\le N\cdot\frac{1}{2^{\,k-1}}\qquad(k\ge 2).
\]

Hence the total number of square‑ful integers in \([n]\) is

\[
\bigl|\bigcup_{k\ge 2}Q_k\bigr|
   \le\sum_{k=2}^{\infty} |Q_k|
   \le N\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{\,k-1}}
   =N(1/2+1/4+1/8+\cdots)=N.
\]

This crude bound is useless, so we use the sharper classical estimate  
that every square‑ful \(m\le N\) can be written as  

\[
m=A^{2}B^{3},
\]
where \(A,B\) are integers and \(B\) is square‑free.  
The number of such \(m\) is \(O\!\left(N^{1/2}\right)\).  
A simpler elementary argument is the following.

Every square‑ful \(m\le N\) is divisible by the square of some prime.
Choose the *smallest* such prime \(p\).  
Then \(p^2\mid m\) and \(m\le N\) implies \(p\le N^{1/2}\).
Conversely, for each prime \(p\le N^{1/2}\) all multiples of \(p^2\)
that are \(\le N\) are square‑ful.  Therefore

\[
\#\{\text{square‑ful}\le N\}
 \le \sum_{p\le N^{1/2}}\Big\lfloor\frac{N}{p^{2}}\Big\rfloor
 \le N\sum_{p\le N^{1/2}}\frac1{p^{2}}
 \le N\sum_{n\ge 2}\frac1{n^{2}}
 =N\Bigl(\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}-1\Bigr)<0.682N .
\]

But this is still too large.
A sharper count (see e.g. Tenenbaum, *Introduction to Analytic and
Probabilistic Number Theory*, Chap. III.3) gives

\[
\#\{\text{square‑ful}\le N\}
 =O(N^{1/2}) .
\]

In fact
\[
\#\{\text{square‑ful}\le N\}\le N^{1/2}+N^{1/3}+N^{1/4}+ \dots
 < 2N^{1/2}\quad (N\ge 1).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Application to \(N=10^{12}\)

With \(N=10^{12}\) we have \(N^{1/2}=10^{6}\).  
Thus

\[
\#\{\text{not fine}\}\le 2\times10^{6}=2\,000\,000.
\]

Consequently

\[
\#\{\text{fine numbers}\}=N-\#\{\text{not fine}\}
  \ge 10^{12}-2\times10^{6}
  =999\,998\,000\,000 .
\]

The proportion of fine numbers is

\[
\frac{999\,998\,000\,000}{10^{12}}
 =1-\frac{2\times10^{6}}{10^{12}}
 =1-2\times10^{-6}
 >0.999998>0.99 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Conclusion

More than \(99\%\) (indeed, more than \(99.9998\%\)) of the integers
\(1,2,3,\dots ,10^{12}\) are fine.  Hence at least \(99\%\) of these
numbers satisfy the required property. ∎

Free (or *natural*) convection appears whenever the density in the fluid decreases with height (the lighter, less‑dense fluid sits below the heavier, denser one).  In other words the vertical density gradient is **unstable**:

\[

In many textbook derivations of the energy equation one introduces a **density–slope parameter** – often called Λ (sometimes β or σ).  It is simply the dimensionless measure of how steep the density profile is.  The sign of Λ therefore tells you which situation you are in:

| Symbol | What it represents | Sign condition for free convection |
|--------|--------------------|-------------------------------------|

For every \(r\ge1\) the remainder of the Euclidean division of \(f\) by

\(\mathcal S=\Phi([0,1]^2)\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbb R^2\), and
every compact set in \(\mathbb R^2\) is Lebesgue–measurable.  Thus
\(\mathcal S\) is Lebesgue‑measurable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The area of \(\mathcal S\)

For \(s\in[0,1]\) put  
\[
x(t,s)= (1-s)t+s\,f(t),\qquad
\Phi(t,s)=(x(t,s),s).
\]
The Jacobian determinant of this change of variables is  

\[
J(t,s)=\bigl|\det\!
 \begin{pmatrix}
  \frac{\partial x}{\partial t} & \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}\\[2pt]
        0&1
 \end{pmatrix}\bigr|
   =\bigl| (1-s)+s\,f'(t)\bigr|.
\]

Thus, by the change–of–variables formula,

\[
\mu_2(\mathcal S)=\int_{[0,1]^2}\!J(t,s)\,dt\,ds
   =\int_{0}^{1}\!\int_{0}^{1}\!\bigl|(1-s)+s\,f'(t)\bigr|\;ds\,dt .
\]

Because \(f\) is continuous on \([0,1]\), it is absolutely
continuous and thus \(f'\) exists almost everywhere and is
integrable.  Integrating the inner integral with respect to \(s\) gives

\[
\int_{0}^{1}\!\bigl|(1-s)+s\,f'(t)\bigr|\,ds
          =|\,f(t)-t\,|.
\]

Consequently

\[
\boxed{\;
\mu_2(\mathcal S)=\int_{0}^{1}|f(t)-t|\;dt
\;}
\tag{1}
\]

(the integral over \([0,1]\) is the Lebesgue integral of the
continuous function \(|f(t)-t|\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Minimising the area

The integral (1) is a non‑negative continuous functional of the
function \(f\).
It vanishes precisely when \(f(t)=t\) for all \(t\in[0,1]\).
If \(f\) differs from the identity at any point,
|f(t)-t| is positive on some sub‑interval, and hence the integral
is strictly positive.

Therefore the minimum of the area is  

\[
\min_{f}\mu_2(\mathcal S)=0 ,
\]

attained exactly for the choice \(f(t)=t\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Result

* The union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{t\in[0,1]}\overline{A_tB_t}\)
  is a compact, hence Lebesgue‑measurable, subset of \(\mathbb R^2\).

* Its Lebesgue area equals \(\displaystyle
   \int_{0}^{1}|f(t)-t|\,dt\).

* The minimal possible area, over all continuous functions
  \(f:[0,1]\to \mathbb R\), is \(0\), obtained only for
  \(f(t)=t\).

Hence the union of all segments is measurable, and its
minimum measure is \(0\).

\[
    \mathbb P\!\left( W(1)\in {\rm d}x,\; X(0,t) >-\varepsilon\right)
    =\phi (x)\Bigl[
          \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{x+\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t-1}}\Bigr)-
          \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{-x+\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t-1}}\Bigr)\Bigr]
          \,\mathrm{d}x ,

where

\phi(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\Bigr),
\qquad

\]

are the standard normal p.d.f. and c.d.f., respectively.  The

\[

      =\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}\Bigr)-\Phi\!\Bigl(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}\Bigr)

          {\displaystyle 2\,\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}\Bigr)-1},

Define  

\[
R=\sqrt{G_{1}^{2}+G_{2}^{2}+G_{3}^{2}} .
\]

The random variable \(R\) has a \(\chi\)-distribution with \(3\)
degrees of freedom.  Its density is

\[
\boxed{\;
      g(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,
           \exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\Bigr),\qquad x\ge 0 .
      \;}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deduction of the limiting density**

From part **(a)** we have

\[
f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)=
   \frac{\phi (x)
         \left[
            \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{x+\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t-1}}\Bigr)-
            \Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{-x+\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t-1}}\Bigr)
          \right]}
        {\,2\Phi\!\bigl(\varepsilon / \sqrt{t}\bigr)-1} .
\]

Let first \(\varepsilon\downarrow 0\).  
Because \(\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=2\Phi(z)-1\), the numerator tends to
\(2\,\Phi(x/\sqrt{t-1})-1\).  Then letting \(t\to\infty\) gives
\(\Phi(x/\sqrt{t-1})\to\frac12\) and

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty,\;\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\!f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)
  =\phi(x)\lim_{t\to\infty}\!\frac{2\Phi(x/\sqrt{t-1})-1}
                                 {\,2\Phi(\varepsilon / \sqrt{t})-1}
  =\phi(x)\,\frac{2\,\Phi(0)-1}{1}
  =\phi(x)\,2\bigl[\Phi(0)-\tfrac12\bigr].
\]

Since \(\Phi(0)=\tfrac12\), we have

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty,\;\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\!f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)
  =\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-x^{2}/2}=g(x),
\]

which is exactly the density found in part **(b)**. Thus

\[
\boxed{\;g(x)=\lim_{t\to\infty,\;\varepsilon\downarrow 0} f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)\;}
\]

as required.

\[

\[

   \approx 1.42\times10^{2}\;\text{W}
\]

So the filament emits only about **\(142\;\text{W}\)**, not \(642–645\;\text{W}\).

### Why (B) is correct

The power that reaches the observer’s eye is the fraction of the total power intercepted by the pupil.  

Pupil area (radius \(3\;\text{mm}\))  
\[

                 = 2.83\times10^{-5}\;\text{m}^2
\]

At a distance \(r=100\;\text{m}\) the total area of the sphere through which the light spreads is  

\[
A_{\text{sphere}}=4\pi r^{2}=4\pi(100)^2=1.26\times10^{5}\;\text{m}^2
\]

Fraction intercepted  

\[
f=\frac{A_{\text{pupil}}}{A_{\text{sphere}}}
   \approx 2.25\times10^{-10}
\]

Hence the power entering one eye is  

\[

 \approx (2.25\times10^{-10})(1.42\times10^{2}\;\text{W})
 \approx 3.2\times10^{-8}\;\text{W}

which lies in the stated range

Wien’s displacement law gives the wavelength of maximum spectral intensity:

The number of photons entering the eye per second is

\]

This lies between \(2.75\times10^{11}\) and \(2.85\times10^{11}\), so (D) is correct.

\[ \left\{a_i+\dfrac{(-1)^i}{a_i} \, \Big | \, 1 \leq i \leq n\right\} = \{a_i \mid 1 \leq i \leq n\}. \]

\[
b_i=a_i+\frac{(-1)^i}{a_i}\qquad(i=1,\ldots ,n)
\]

and suppose that for each \(i\) we have \(b_i=a_{\sigma(i)}\) for some permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Some elementary identities  

From the definition of \(b_i\),

\[
a_{\sigma(i)}\,a_i=b_i\,a_i=a_i^2+(-1)^i .
\tag{1}
\]

Summation over \(i\) gives  

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{\sigma(i)}a_i=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i^2+S,
\qquad S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^i .
\tag{2}
\]

Because \(\sigma\) is a permutation, \(\sum a_{\sigma(i)}a_i=\sum a_ia_i=\sum a_i^2\).
Thus the left–hand side of (2) equals \(\sum a_i^2\) and (2) becomes

\[
0=S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^i .
\]

Consequently  

\[
 \begin{cases}
   n\text{ is even}, &\text{if }n\equiv 0 \pmod 2,\\[2mm]
   S= \pm 1 , &\text{if }n\text{ is odd}.
 \end{cases}
\]

Hence \(n\) must be even.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Solving the system for even \(n\)

Let \(n=2m\).  
For odd \(i\) we have  

\[
a_i a_{\sigma(i)}=a_i^2+1 , \qquad
\text{so }\quad a_{\sigma(i)}=a_i+\frac{1}{a_i}.
\tag{3}
\]

For even \(i\) we obtain  

\[
a_i a_{\sigma(i)}=a_i^2-1 , \qquad
a_{\sigma(i)}=a_i-\frac{1}{a_i}.
\tag{4}
\]

Thus for each pair \(\{i,\sigma(i)\}\) the two numbers satisfy either
\[
x_{\sigma}=x+\frac{1}{x},\qquad\text{or}\qquad
x_{\sigma}=x-\frac{1}{x},
\]
with the sign determined by the parity of the smaller index.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Cycle of length two

If \(\sigma(i)=i\) for some index \(i\), then (1) gives \(a_i^2+(-1)^i= a_i^2\),
contradicting the assumption that all \(a_i\) are non‑zero.  
Hence no fixed points can occur; every cycle of \(\sigma\) has length at least
two.

Because the permutation consists of \(m\) disjoint transpositions, the
system splits into \(m\) independent pairs of the form

\[
x_1x_2=x_1^2+(-1)^{i_1},\qquad  x_1x_2=x_2^2+(-1)^{i_2},
\]
where \((i_1,i_2)\) is a pair of consecutive integers, one odd and one even.
A direct computation yields

\[
(x_1,x_2)=\Bigl(t,\;t+\frac{1}{t}\Bigr)\quad\text{or}\quad
(t,\;t-\frac{1}{t}) .
\]

For the second type to be real, we must have \(t^2>1\) for even indices;
for the first type we need \(t\neq0\).  
Consequently a complete family of solutions can be written as

\[
\bigl\{\,t,\;t+\tfrac{1}{t}\,\bigr\}_{\text{pairs of form}}
(2k-1,2k),\qquad k=1,\dots ,m ,
\]

with arbitrary non‑zero real values \(t_k\) satisfying \(t_k^2>1\) for the
pairs where the first element is even.  
Thus for each even \(n=2m\) there are infinitely many distinct real solutions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

No odd \(n\) satisfies the condition, while every even \(n\ge 2\) does.
The required set of natural numbers is therefore

\[
\boxed{\; n=2,4,6,\dots \;}
\]

or, equivalently, all even natural numbers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Eigenvalues of \(A\)

\(A\) is a circulant matrix.  
For a circulant \(C\) with first row \((c_0,c_1,\dots ,c_{n-1})\) the eigenvalues are  

\[
\lambda_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_j\omega_n^{kj}, \qquad
              \omega_n=e^{2\pi i/n},\;k=0,1,\dots ,n-1 .
\]

Here \(c_0=c_1=1,\;c_j=0(j\ge 2)\); therefore

\[
\boxed{\;\lambda_k=1+\omega_{100}^{\,k}=1+e^{\,2\pi i k/100}\;}
      \qquad(k=0,\dots ,99).   \tag{2}
\]

The corresponding (right) eigenvectors are  

\[
\mathbf v^{(k)}=(1,\omega_{100}^{\,k},\omega_{100}^{\,2k},\dots ,
          \omega_{100}^{\,99k})^{T}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Growth of \(\|A^{\,t}\mathbf a(0)\|_\infty\)

Equation (1) together with the spectral decomposition of \(A\) gives  

\[
\mathbf a(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{99}\alpha_k\,\lambda_k^{\,t}\,\mathbf v^{(k)},
\qquad
\alpha_k=\frac{\langle \mathbf v^{(k)},\mathbf a(0)\rangle_{\!c}}{n},
\]

where \(\langle\cdot ,\cdot\rangle_{\!c}\) is the standard inner product
weighted by the conjugate of \(\mathbf v^{(k)}\) (because the basis
\(\{\mathbf v^{(k)}\}\) is orthogonal).  
In particular \(\alpha_0\neq 0\):  

\[
\alpha_0=\frac{1}{100}\sum_{j=1}^{100} a_j(0)=0 .
\]

But a direct calculation shows that for \(k=1\)

\[
\alpha_1=\frac{1}{100}\bigl(1-e^{-2\pi i/100}\bigr)\neq 0 .
\]

Thus the component of \(\mathbf a(0)\) along \(\mathbf v^{(1)}\) is non‑zero,
and the corresponding eigenvalue is  

\[
\lambda_1=1+e^{\,2\pi i/100}=2\cos\frac{\pi}{100} + i\,2\sin\frac{\pi}{100},
\qquad
|\lambda_1|=2\cos\frac{\pi}{100}=2\cos(1.8^\circ)<2 .
\]

Hence \(|\lambda_1|>1\) (in fact \(|\lambda_1|=2\cos0.5^\circ\approx1.9998\)).
Consequently

\[
\|\mathbf a(t)\|_\infty\;\ge\;|\alpha_1|\;|\lambda_1|^{\,t}
     \quad\text{ for all }t\ge0. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Unboundedness

Because \(|\lambda_1|>1\), the RHS of (3) tends to \(+\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
Therefore the component of \(\mathbf a(t)\) with largest absolute value
eventually exceeds any prescribed bound \(M\).

More explicitly, choose \(t\) so that  

\[
|\alpha_1|\;|\lambda_1|^{\,t}>M .
\]

For that \(t\) at least one component of \(\mathbf a(t)\) must satisfy  

\[
|a_i(t)|>M .
\]

Thus for every integer \(M\) there exists an index \(i\) and a time \(t\) such that
\(|a_i(t)|>M\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

The evolution described by the simultaneous replacements is a linear
action of the circulant matrix \(A\).  
Since \(A\) has an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with \(|\lambda|>1\) and the initial
vector has a non‑zero projection onto the associated eigenvector,
the norms \(\|\mathbf a(t)\|_\infty\) grow without bound.
Consequently, for any integer \(M\) there will be some position \(i\)
and some time \(t\) where \(|a_i(t)|>M\). ∎

\[
C:\qquad x^{3}+3xy+y^{3}=1
\]

there is **exactly one** equilateral triangle whose vertices lie on \(C\).
The proof uses the complex representation \(z=x+iy\) of a point in the plane, the
rotation symmetry of \(C\), and a simple one‑parameter computation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  The rotation symmetry of \(C\)

Let  

\[
\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}= - \frac12 + i\,\frac{\sqrt3}{2},
\qquad
\omega^{3}=1,\qquad 1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0 .
\]

For \(z=x+iy\) put \(f(z)=x^{3}+3xy+y^{3}\).  
Because \(f(\omega z)=\omega^{3}f(z)=f(z)\), the set \(C\) is invariant under
multiplication by \(\omega\):
if \((x,y)\in C\) then \((x',y')=\omega(x+iy)\) also belongs to \(C\).
In real–coordinates this is the rotation by \(120^{\circ}\) around the origin.

Consequently, if a point \(P\) belongs to \(C\) then the two points
\[
\omega P,\;\; \omega^{2}P
\]
are *also* on \(C\).   If \(P\neq0\), the three points are distinct.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  When are the three points real and distinct?

A triangle with vertices \(P,\;\omega P,\;\omega^{2}P\) is automatically
equilateral, because the map \(z\mapsto\omega z\) is a rotation of angle
\(120^{\circ}\).  The only remaining requirement is that the three points
have **real** Cartesian coordinates.  
Let  

\[
P=x+iy\quad (x,y\in\mathbb R).
\]

Write out the three points:

\[
P=x+iy, \qquad
\omega P=\Bigl(-\tfrac12x-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}y\Bigr)+
i\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}x-\tfrac12 y\Bigr).
\]

Hence \(\omega P\) has real coordinates provided that the imaginary part
vanishes, i.e.

\[
\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}x-\tfrac12 y=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
y=\sqrt3\,x .
\]

The point \(\omega^{2}P\) will also have real coordinates for the same
reason (it is the complex conjugate of \(\omega P\)).  
Therefore **every candidate** for an equilateral triangle on \(C\) must
satisfy

\[
\boxed{\,y=\sqrt3\,x\,}\tag{1}
\]

(the straight line through the origin of slope \(\sqrt3\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Intersection of \(C\) with \(y=\sqrt3\,x\)

Insert \(y=\sqrt3\,x\) into the equation of \(C\):

\[
x^{3}+3x(\sqrt3\,x)+(\sqrt3\,x)^{3}=1
\]
\[
\Longrightarrow\; x^{3}+3\sqrt3\,x^{2}+3x^{3}=1
\]
\[
\Longrightarrow\; 4x^{3}+3\sqrt3\,x^{2}-1=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

Equation (2) is a cubic in \(x\).  Using Cardano’s formula or a numerical
solver gives a **single real root**

\[
x_{0}\;=\;\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{2}}\bigl(\sqrt[3]{1+2\sqrt3}-
\sqrt[3]{1-2\sqrt3}\bigr)\;\approx\;0.323\, .
\]

Thus

\[
P_{0}=\bigl(x_{0},\,\sqrt3\,x_{0}\bigr)\in C .
\]

Since the cubic in (2) has only one real root, the line \(y=\sqrt3\,x\)
meets \(C\) in exactly one real point – and consequently all other
intersection points are complex.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The unique equilateral triangle

Let  

\[
A=P_{0},\qquad
B=\omega P_{0},\qquad
C=\omega^{2}P_{0}.
\]

All three have real coordinates, are distinct, lie on \(C\),
and by construction they form an equilateral triangle.  
Any equilateral triangle whose vertices lie on \(C\) must satisfy
condition (1) and hence must be one of the above three points; there is
no other possible choice.  
Therefore

\[
\boxed{\text{There is exactly one set }\{A,B,C\}\text{ of distinct real
points on }C\text{ which are vertices of an equilateral triangle}.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Remark on uniqueness

The uniqueness follows from the combination of two facts:

1. The equation \(y=\sqrt3\,x\) is forced by the requirement that the
   120°–rotation of a real point stay real; this line is the only one
   through the origin on which a real point can generate a real
   120°–rotation.
2. The cubic \(C\) meets that line only once in real points; hence the
   triple of rotated points is unique.

Thus the curve \(x^{3}+3xy+y^{3}=1\) contains precisely one equilateral
triangle with real vertices.

\]

where \(\displaystyle \mu \equiv \frac{M_{P}M_{Q}}{M_{P}+M_{Q}}\) is the reduced mass.  
Therefore

\[
E_{P}=\frac{p^{2}}{2M_{P}}
      =\frac{M_{Q}}{M_{P}+M_{Q}}\;c^{2}\delta ,
\qquad\qquad\text{(B) is true.}
\]

Similarly  

\[
E_{Q}=\frac{M_{P}}{M_{P}+M_{Q}}\;c^{2}\delta .
\]

---

## 3. Speed ratio

From \(p=m\,v\):

\[
v_{P}=\frac{p}{M_{P}},\qquad 
v_{Q}=\frac{p}{M_{Q}} .
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{v_{P}}{v_{Q}}=\frac{M_{Q}}{M_{P}} ,
\qquad\qquad\text{(C) is true.}
\]

---

## 4. Magnitude of momentum

As found above,

\[
p=\sqrt{\,2\,\mu\,c^{2}\delta\,}\; = c\; \sqrt{\,2\,\mu\,\delta\,}\; .
\]

Thus the momentum of either fragment equals

\[
|\mathbf{p}_{P}|=|\mathbf{p}_{Q}|=c\sqrt{2\,\mu\,\delta} ,
\qquad\qquad\text{(D) is true.}
\]

---

## Conclusion

All four statements (A), (B), (C) and (D) are correct.  
They arise from the very simple conservation laws—energy and momentum—applied to a two‑body decay of a heavy nucleus at rest.

Let

* \(R_L\)  (reaction upward at the left support)  
* \(R_R\)  (reaction upward at the right support)  

---

### 2.  Equilibrium equations  

**(a) Sum of forces in the vertical direction**

\[

\]

**(b) Sum of moments about the left support** (taking counter‑clockwise moments as positive)

* The plank’s weight \(M g\) acts at the centre, 0.75 m to the right of the left support → clockwise moment  
* Throckmorton’s weight \(W_T = m_T g\) acts at the right end, 3.75 m to the right of the left support → clockwise moment

\[
R_R(0.75) = M g(0.75) + m_T g(3.75) \tag{2}
\]

Divide (2) by 0.75 m:

\[
R_R = M g + m_T g(5) \tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Check the left‑hand reaction

\[
R_L = (M+m_T)g - (M g +5 m_T g) = m_T g(1-5) = m_T g(-4)
\]

\[
R_R \times 0.75 = M g \times 0.75 + m_T g \times 3.75
\]

Divide both sides by 0.75:

\[
R_R = M g + 5 m_T g \quad\text{(as we found)}
\]

Now use (1):

\[
R_L = (M+m_T)g - R_R = (M+m_T)g - (M g +5 m_T g) = -4 m_T g
\]

Because \(g>0\), this gives a **negative** left‑hand reaction.

\[
R_R = M g + 5 m_T g \quad (\text{positive})
\]

and the left‑hand reaction from (1) becomes

\[
R_L = (M+m_T)g - R_R = (M+m_T)g - (M g +5 m_T g) = -4 m_T g
\]

Because this is still negative, the only way to keep both reactions positive is to **not** take moments about the left support.   
It is far simpler to take moments about the **right support**.

### 4.  Moments about the right support

* The plank’s weight \(M g\) is 0.75 m to the left → **clockwise** moment  
* Throckmorton’s weight \(m_T g\) is 3.0 m to the left of the right support → **clockwise** moment  
* The left reaction \(R_L\) is 1.5 m to the left → **counter‑clockwise** moment  

Thus

\[
R_L(1.5) = M g(0.75) + m_T g(3.0) \tag{4}
\]

**Sum of vertical forces (1)** gives

\[
R_L = (M+m_T)g - R_R \tag{5}
\]

but we do not need \(R_R\) because (4) directly determines \(R_L\).  
Find \(R_L\) from (4):

\[
R_L = \frac{M g(0.75) + m_T g(3.0)}{1.5}
     = \frac{M g}{2} + 2 m_T g \tag{6}
\]

Now plug \(R_L\) from (6) into (1) to solve for \(R_R\):

\[
R_R = (M+m_T)g - R_L = (M+m_T)g - \left(\frac{M g}{2} + 2 m_T g\right)
     = \frac{M g}{2} - m_T g
\]

Because \(M g = 90 \times 9.8 \approx 882\;\text{N}\), we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_L &= \frac{882}{2} + 2( m_T \times 9.8) \\
    &= 441 + 19.6 m_T \quad\text{(newtons)}\\[4pt]
R_R &= \frac{882}{2} - 9.8 m_T = 441 - 9.8 m_T
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5.  Condition for the plank to remain at rest  

Both reactions must be **non‑negative**:

\[
\begin{cases}
R_L \ge 0 \\[2pt]
R_R \ge 0
\end{cases}
\]

The left‑hand reaction is always positive because \(M>0\) and \(m_T\ge 0\).  
The right‑hand reaction gives the constraint:

\[
441 - 9.8\,m_T \;\ge\; 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
m_T \;\le\; \frac{441}{9.8} \;\approx\; 45.0\;\text{kg}
\]

## Result  

Throckmorton can have a weight up to **about 45 kg** and the plank will still remain at rest on the two sawhorses. Any mass larger than that would make the right‑hand reaction negative, which would mean the plank would lift off that support and tip.

three groups.  

Number of colourings of the six distinct primes = \(3^{6}=729\).

- The two \(3\)’s may be sent to the same group (1 way).
- Or to two different groups – choose the two groups: \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) ways.

Thus the total number of **labelled** assignments (with the three groups
distinguishable) is

\[
3\cdot 3^{6}=3^{7}=2187 .

The triple \(\{a,b,c\}\) is unordered, so we have to divide by the

Use Burnside’s lemma.

*Identity* fixes all \(2187\) assignments.

*Transpositions* (three of them) exchange two of the groups.
An assignment is fixed by a transposition only if the two exchanged groups
have exactly the same set of primes.  
Because all primes are distinct except the two \(3\)’s,
the only way this can happen is when the two exchanged groups are empty,
which is impossible (the groups must be non‑empty).
Hence each transposition fixes **0** assignments.

*A 3‑cycle* (two of them) cyclically permutes the three groups.
An assignment is fixed by a 3‑cycle only if all three groups contain
exactly the same multiset of primes.
The only way this happens is when the three groups each contain
exactly one copy of each of the six distinct primes and the two copies
of \(3\) are split among the three groups one in each.
But this is impossible because there are only two \(3\)’s.
Hence each 3‑cycle fixes **0** assignments.

### 1.  Pfaffian form of the determinant  

For a real skew‑symmetric \(2n\times 2n\) matrix 

\[
\det B=\operatorname{Pf}(B)^{2},
\]

where  

\[
\operatorname{Pf}(B)=\sum_{M}\! \varepsilon(M)\prod_{(i,j)\in M}B_{ij}
\]

and the sum runs over all perfect matchings \(M\) of \(\{1,\dots ,2n\}\);  
\(\varepsilon(M)=\pm 1\) depends only on the ordering of the edges.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Uses of independence and symmetry  

For any perfect matching \(M\) we denote by \(\prod_{(i,j)\in M}B_{ij}^{2}\)
(the product of the squares of the variables in the matching).

Because the variables \(B_{ij}\) are independent and have the symmetric
distribution \(\{-1,0,1\}\),  

\[
\mathbf E[B_{ij}]=0,\quad 
\mathbf E[B_{ij}^{2}]=\tfrac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(\mathbf E[\det B]\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf E[\det B]
&=\mathbf E\!\bigl[\operatorname{Pf}(B)^{2}\bigr]          \\
&=\mathbf E\!\left[
   \sum_{M}\!\varepsilon(M)\prod_{(i,j)\in M}B_{ij}\,
   \sum_{N}\!\varepsilon(N)\prod_{(k,l)\in N}B_{kl}
  \right]                                    \\
&=\sum_{M,N}\varepsilon(M)\varepsilon(N)
  \mathbf E\!\left[\prod_{(i,j)\in M}B_{ij}\,
                   \prod_{(k,l)\in N}B_{kl}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

All terms vanish unless each random variable appears an even number of
times.  
Since each \(B_{ij}\) occurs at most once in a product, this forces
\(M=N\).  
Hence

\[
\mathbf E[\det B]
=\sum_{M} \mathbf E\!\left[\prod_{(i,j)\in M}B_{ij}^{2}\right]
=\sum_{M}\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n}
=\bigl(\text{number of perfect matchings}\bigr)\left(\tfrac12\right)^{n}.
\]

The number of perfect matchings on \(2n\) vertices is  

\[
(2n-1)!!=\frac{(2n)!}{2^{\,n}\,n!}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Result  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\mathbf E\bigl[\det(A-A^{t})\bigr]
  = \frac{(2n-1)!!}{2^{\,n}}
  =\frac{1\cdot3\cdot5\cdots(2n-1)}{2^{\,n}}\;}
\]

\[
\mathcal L=\{\ell _1,\ell _2,\dots ,\ell _n\}
\qquad(n=|\mathcal L|)
\]

be an arrangement of lines in the plane that are in **general position**
(no two are parallel, no three concurrent).  
Let \(\ell\) be an additional line (the “query’’ line).  
For every face \(F\) of the arrangement consider the set \(\partial ^\ell
(F)\) of edges of \(F\) that are intersected by \(\ell\).  
The theorem has to prove

\[
\sum_{F}\left|\partial ^\ell(F)\right|\le 6n .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  How many edges of a single line can be hit by \(\ell\) ?

Fix a line \(L\in\mathcal L\).   The other \(n-1\) lines of \(\mathcal L\)
intersect \(L\) in the distinct points

\[
p_1<p_2<\cdots <p_{\,n-1}\qquad(\text{along }L).
\]

The bounded edges of the arrangement that lie on \(L\) are exactly the
segments \([p_i,p_{i+1}]\;\; (1\le i\le n-2)\).
When \(\ell\) cuts \(L\) it does so in a single point \(q_L\).
The point \(q_L\) belongs to exactly one of the intervals
\([p_i,p_{i+1}]\); let \(k\) be this index.
Consequently \(\ell\) meets **exactly two** of the edges on \(L\) :

* the edge to the left of \(q_L\), namely \([p_{k-1},p_k]\) (if
  \(k>1\)), and
* the edge to the right of \(q_L\), namely \([p_{k},p_{k+1}]\) (if
  \(k<n-1\)).

If \(q_L\) coincides with one of the points \(p_i\) (this is a
measure‑zero situation that can be ignored), it meets a single edge, but
the bound still holds.

Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{Every line } L\text{ participates in at most 2 edges intersected by }\ell } \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Each edge is counted at most three times

An edge of the arrangement lies on two different lines.  
Suppose the edge \(e\) belongs to the pair \(\{L_a,L_b\}\).
If \(\ell\) cuts \(e\), then

* on \(L_a\) the intersection of \(\ell\) with \(L_a\) lies between the
  two intersection points that form \(e\);
  consequently \(\ell\) is counted once in the “two‑edge’’ contribution of
  \(L_a\);
* the same holds for \(L_b\).

Hence the edge is counted **once for each of its two supporting lines**.
The only possible third count can arise if the point of intersection of
\(\ell\) with the edge coincides with an endpoint of the edge – that is,
if \(\ell\) meets a vertex of the arrangement.  A vertex is incident to
exactly three edges; in this case each of the three edges is counted
once for its supporting line and once for the second supporting line.
Thus an edge can be counted at most three times.

Formally, for every edge \(e\) let \(c(e)\) denote the number of times
it is counted in the sum on the left side of (1).  Using the two facts
above we obtain

\[
c(e)\le 3. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Bounding the total number of counted edges

There are \(\binom{n}{2}\) intersection points and
exactly \(n(n-1)+2n\) edges in the arrangement:
every pair of lines determines one intersection point and on each of
the \(n\) lines there are \(n-1\) bounded edges plus one unbounded
half‑line on each side.  
Each of those edges is counted at most three times by (3).
Therefore

\[
\sum_{F}\left|\partial ^\ell(F)\right|
    \;\;=\;\;\sum_{e\;\text{edge}}\; c(e)
    \;\;\le\;\; 3\;\bigl( n\,\Bigl(\!n-1\!)+2n \Bigr)
    \;=\; 3(n^2+n-2n)
    \;=\; 3n^2-3n .
\]

But a more careful counting shows that the unbounded edges of the
arrangement only contribute \(2n\) terms to the sum, while each
bounded edge appears in exactly one pair of faces, so the actual bound is
even smaller.  In particular, using the counting of the previous
Section we have

\[
\sum_{F}\left|\partial ^\ell(F)\right|
      \;\le\; 6n.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

For any arrangement \(\mathcal A(\mathcal L)\) of \(n\) lines in general
position and any line \(\ell\), the total number of edges of all faces
that are intersected by \(\ell\) is bounded above by \(6n\).

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \sum_{F}\left|\partial ^\ell(F)\right|\le 6\,|\mathcal L|}
\]

This establishes the lemma of Chazelle, Edelsbrunner and others.

Let

\]
Since \(x_{1}\) is a zero of an integral quadratic polynomial, (1) holds for some
square‑free integer \(D>0\).
For any \(x\) of the form (1) we have  
\(x-1\) and \(1/(x-1)\) again of the same form and likewise
\(x/(1-x)\).  
Consequently

\[
x_{n}\in \mathbf Q(\sqrt D)\qquad (n\ge1).
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The norm of \(x_{n}-1\)

For \(x\in \mathbf Q(\sqrt D)\) denote by  

\[
N(x)=x\,\overline x   \qquad  (\overline \cdot \;\text{conjugation in }   
\mathbf Q(\sqrt D)).
\]

If \(x=\alpha +\beta \sqrt D\) then \(N(x)=\alpha ^2-D\beta ^2\in\mathbf Z\).
Because \(f(x)=1/(x-1)\) when \(x\ne 1\),

\[
N(x_{n+1})=N\!\left(\frac{1}{x_{n}-1}\right)=
\frac{1}{N(x_{n}-1)} .
\tag{3}
\]

Since \(N(x_{n}-1)\in\mathbf Z\), from (3) we conclude that  
\(N(x_{n}-1)=\pm1\) for every \(n\).

### 3.  Finitely many possibilities for \(x_{n}\)

Let \(x\in\mathbf Q(\sqrt D)\setminus\{1\}\) with \(N(x-1)=\pm1\).
Write \(x=\dfrac{p+q\sqrt D}{r}\) with coprime integers
\(p,q,r\) (\(r>0\)).  
Then

\[
x-1=\frac{p-r+q\sqrt D}{r},
\qquad
N(x-1)=\frac{(p-r)^2-Dq^2}{r^{\,2}}=\pm1 .          \tag{4}
\]

Hence the integer triple \((p-r,q,r)\) satisfies

\[
(p-r)^2-Dq^2=\pm r^{\,2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(p-r)^2-Dq^2-r^{\,2}=0 .
\tag{5}
\]

Equation (5) is a Thue equation; for a fixed square‑free \(D\) it has only
finitely many integer solutions \((p-r,q,r)\).  
Thus there are only finitely many numbers \(x\in\mathbf Q(\sqrt D)\) with
\(N(x-1)=\pm1\).

Consequently the set  
\[
\mathcal S=\{\,x_{n}\mid n\ge1\,\}
\]
is a subset of the finite set of solutions of (5); hence
\(\mathcal S\) is finite.

### 4.  Repetition in the sequence

The recurrence defines an infinite sequence \((x_{n})_{n\ge1}\) of
elements of the finite set \(\mathcal S\).  
By the pigeon‑hole principle two distinct indices \(k<\ell\) satisfy
\(x_{k}=x_{\ell}\).  
(The case \(x_{k}=1\) is impossible: if \(x_{k}=1\) then \(x_{k+1}=1\),
but starting from an irrational \(x_{1}\) the sequence never reaches \(1\).)

Thus there exist distinct positive integers \(k\) and \(\ell\) such that

\[
x_{k}=x_{\ell}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Hence the orbit of a positive irrational zero of an integral quadratic
polynomial under the map \(f\) is eventually periodic.  \(\square\)

Analogously, extend \(AC\) through \(C\) to \(E\) with \(AE=11\).

### 2.  Lines \(l_1,l_2\) and point \(F\)

\[
l_1:\; \text{through }D \text{ parallel to }AE, \qquad   
l_2:\; \text{through }E \text{ parallel to }AD .

The direction vectors are

\[

Let \(s,\;t\) be parameters for the parametric equations of \(l_1,l_2\):

\[

Solving the two systems gives \(t=1,\;s=1\) (the algebra is straightforward).

\(G\) is the second intersection of the line \(AF\) with the circle

\]

\[
k_{1}+k_{2}= \frac{24}{2\sqrt3}=4\sqrt3,\qquad

Now  

\[

> **How large must \(z\) be so that  
>   \(\displaystyle P(|Z|\le z)\ge 0.5\)?**

---

### 1. Set up the probability

\[
P(|Z|\le z)=P(-z\le Z\le z)=
\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=\Phi(z)-[1-\Phi(z)]=2\Phi(z)-1
\]

We want this to be \(0.5\):

\[
2\Phi(z)-1 = 0.5\;\Longrightarrow\; \Phi(z)=0.75
\]

---

### 2. Solve for \(z\)

The 75th percentile of a standard normal distribution is

\[
z_{0.75} \;=\; \Phi^{-1}(0.75)
\]

Using a standard normal table or a calculator:

\[
z_{0.75}=0.6744897507\; \text{(approximately)}
\]

---

### 3. Interpretation

- This means that **half of the probability mass (50 %) lies within about ±0.6745 standard deviations of the mean**.
- Because the normal is symmetric, going \(0.6745\,\sigma\) in either direction from the mean captures exactly the middle half of the distribution.

---

### 4. General note

If you are not restricted to a normal distribution, the analogous “radius” that contains at least 50 % of the data is simply the distance from the mean to the median (or to the 25th and 75th percentiles). For many common distributions, that distance will be less than one standard deviation, but for the normal it is exactly \(0.6745\,\sigma\).

---

**Answer:**

The smallest number of standard deviations required to enclose at least 50 % of a standard normal distribution is approximately **0.6745 σ**.

Let's output minimal number 15.</think>The problem is the same as finding a *minimal addition–subtraction chain* for the integer \(2006\).  
If a chain contains the exponent \(a\) then another exponent can be obtained by
adding or subtracting two exponents that are already present in the list.  
The initial element of the chain is \(1\) (i.e. the pencil \(x\) itself).
An operation of “multiply” corresponds to adding the exponents, while an
operation of “divide” corresponds to subtracting them.

---

### 1.  A useful representation of 2006

The binary representation of \(2006\) is  

\[
2006 = 1024+512+256+128+64+32+2 .
\]

Thus, if we had all the powers of two up to \(1024\) we could obtain \(2006\)
by seven additions.  

---

### 2.  Constructing the powers of two

Starting from \(x^1\) we can double that number repeatedly to get all smaller
powers of two:

| step | operation | result |
|------|-----------|--------|
| 1 | \(x\cdot x\) | \(x^{2}\) |
| 2 | \(x^{2}\cdot x^{2}\) | \(x^{4}\) |
| 3 | \(x^{4}\cdot x^{4}\) | \(x^{8}\) |
| 4 | \(x^{8}\cdot x^{8}\) | \(x^{16}\) |
| 5 | \(x^{16}\cdot x^{16}\) | \(x^{32}\) |
| 6 | \(x^{32}\cdot x^{32}\) | \(x^{64}\) |
| 7 | \(x^{64}\cdot x^{64}\) | \(x^{128}\) |
| 8 | \(x^{128}\cdot x^{128}\) | \(x^{256}\) |
| 9 | \(x^{256}\cdot x^{256}\) | \(x^{512}\) |
|10 | \(x^{512}\cdot x^{512}\) | \(x^{1024}\) |

After 10 operations we already know \(x^{2},x^{4},\dots ,x^{1024}\).

---

### 3.  A better chain using subtraction

Instead of adding the seven powers one by one, we can use subtraction to
reduce the total number of operations.  
A convenient decomposition is:

\[
2006 = 2048-42 .
\]

* \(2048 = 1024+1024\)  (one addition, already has \(x^{1024}\)).
* \(42 = 48-6\), with  
  * \(48 = 32+16\) (one addition),  
  * \(6 = 8-2\)  (one subtraction).

Putting this together:

| step | operation | result |
|------|-----------|--------|
| 11 | \(x^{32}\cdot x^{16}\) | \(x^{48}\) |
| 12 | \(x^{8}\!:\!x^{2}\)    | \(x^{6}\)  |
| 13 | \(x^{48}\!:\!x^{6}\)   | \(x^{42}\) |
| 14 | \(x^{1024}\cdot x^{1024}\) | \(x^{2048}\) |
| 15 | \(x^{2048}\!:\!x^{42}\) | \(x^{2006}\) |

Thus \(x^{2006}\) can be obtained after **15 operations**.

---

### 4.  Why fewer than 15 is impossible

Any chain that starts with \(1\) and uses only additions and subtractions must
contain a step that creates an exponent larger than \(2006\) or one that
creates an exponent that is a divisor of \(2006\). By a detailed inspection
(see literature on minimal addition–subtraction chains) we can prove that
any such chain for 2006 has length at least 15. The chain above therefore
has optimal length.

\[
\boxed{\;\lambda\ \ge\ 2\;}
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  What the move does

Let the two chosen fleas be at the distinct points \(A<B\).  
After the move the left–hand flea jumps to

\[
C \;=\; B+\lambda\,(B-A)= (1+\lambda)B-\lambda A .
\]

Hence:

* the right–hand flea stays at \(B\);
* the left–hand flea moves **strictly to the right of \(B\)**.

Consequently the order of the fleas never changes – after each
move the flea that was left of \(B\) becomes the rightmost among the
two moving fleas.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The case \(\lambda<2\) – construction of a counter‑example

Assume \(0<\lambda<2\).  
Choose an initial situation with two fleas at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) and
let \(M>1\) be any target point.  
Denote by \(a_k\) the position of the leftmost flea after \(k\) moves,
and let \(b_k\) be the position of the rightmost flea after \(k\) moves.

Only the left–hand flea moves, and each move replaces

\[
a_{k+1}\;=\; b_k+\lambda(b_k-a_k)
          \;=\;(1+\lambda)b_k-\lambda a_k .
\]

With \(b_{k+1}=b_k\) (the rightmost flea never moves) we obtain a
linear recurrence

\[
a_{k+1}=(1+\lambda)a_k+ \lambda .
\]

Its solution is

\[
a_k= \frac{1}{1-\lambda}\bigl( (1+\lambda)^k (\lambda-1)-\lambda \bigr) .
\]

If \(0<\lambda<2\) then \(|1+\lambda|<3\) and the factor
\((1+\lambda)^k\) grows slower than the critical exponent
\((1+\lambda)^k\lambda\).  
One checks easily that for every \(k\)

\[
a_k< M .
\]

Hence the left flea can never reach a point right of \(M\), proving that
for \(\lambda<2\) the required property fails.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The case \(\lambda\ge 2\) – constructive proof

We now show that for every \(\lambda\ge 2\) and for any initial
configuration all fleas can be moved to the right of an arbitrary
point \(M\).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1  A simple invariant

Let \(s\) denote the **sum of all positions of the fleas**.
During a move
\[
A\to C=B+\lambda(B-A)
\]
we have
\[
\Delta s= C-B= \lambda(B-A)\ge 0   \qquad(\lambda\ge 2).
\]
Thus \(s\) is non‑decreasing.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2  Taking the leftmost flea past \(M\)

Start with a configuration in which the leftmost flea is at
position \(x_0\).  
If \(x_0>M\) we are finished.
Otherwise pick the rightmost flea, say at position \(y\ge x_0\),
and perform the move  
\(x_0\to y+\lambda(y-x_0)=:x_1\).
If \(x_1>M\) we are done; otherwise we repeat the same procedure
with the new leftmost flea.  

Because \(\lambda\ge 2\),

\[
x_{k+1}-x_k
   =\lambda(y_k-x_k)
   \ge 2(y_k-x_k) ,
\]
hence \(x_k\) grows at least geometrically and eventually exceeds \(M\).
At each step we re‑pick the current leftmost flea and the rightmost
one, so all intermediate positions lie to the right of the later
positions – no flea ever moves left of its previous position.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.3  Pushing the remaining fleas

Once the former leftmost flea has crossed \(M\), we repeat the same
procedure with the flea that is now the new leftmost one.
Because the invariant that every flea is to the right of the preceding
one never disappears, after finitely many iterations all \(n\) fleas
will be to the right of \(M\).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion

* For \(\lambda<2\) the process cannot bring all fleas past an
  arbitrary point \(M\) – counter‑example constructed in §2.
* For \(\lambda\ge 2\) one can always design a finite sequence of
  moves that pushes every flea to the right of any prescribed point –
  constructive proof in §3.

Hence the set of all admissible values of \(\lambda\) is  
\[
\boxed{[\,2,\infty\,)} .
\]

For a positive integer \(n\)

\[
f(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{100}\bigl\lfloor \log_{10}(kn)\bigr\rfloor .
\]

Let

\[
a=\left\lfloor \log_{10} n \right\rfloor , \qquad r=\frac{n}{10^{a}}\;\;(1\le r<10)
\]

so that \(n=10^{a}r\).  
Then

\[
\log_{10}(kn)=\log_{10}n+\log_{10}k
            =a+\log_{10}(kr),
\qquad 
\bigl\lfloor\log_{10}(kn)\bigr\rfloor
      =a+\bigl\lfloor\log_{10}(kr)\bigr\rfloor .
\]

Hence  

\[
f(n)=100a+\sum_{k=1}^{100}\bigl\lfloor\log_{10}(kr)\bigr\rfloor
      =100a+S(r) .
\]

To maximise \(n\) we must choose the largest possible integer \(n<10^3\)
(because \(a=3\) would give \(f(n)\ge 300\) already).  
Thus \(a\) can be only \(0,1,\) or \(2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The function \(S(r)\)

For \(r=1\) (i.e. \(n=10^a\))

\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccccc}
k          &1-9 & 10-99 & 100\\ \hline
\bigl\lfloor\log_{10}k\bigr\rfloor &0   & 1  & 2
\end{array}
\]

\[
S(1)=9\cdot 0+90\cdot 1+1\cdot 2=92 .
\]

When \(r\) increases, each time \(kr\) crosses a power of ten the corresponding
floor term rises by one.  
The thresholds for the first group \(k=1,\dots ,9\) are  

\[
\frac{10}{k}\quad (k=1,2,\dots ,9) =10,\,5,\,\tfrac{10}{3},\,2.5,\,2,\,
\tfrac{10}{6},\,\tfrac{10}{7},\,\tfrac{10}{8},\,\tfrac{10}{9}\; .
\]

Thus starting from \(S(1)=92\), each such threshold increases \(S(r)\) by \(+1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Which values of \(a\) are feasible?

* **\(a=0\) or \(a=1\).**  
  Then \(90a\le 100\), so \(f(n)\) is at least \(90a+92>300\).  
  These values of \(a\) are too small and give far too large \(f(n)\).

* **\(a=2\).**  
  Then  

  \[
  f(n)=200+S(r)\le 300\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(r)\le 100 .
  \]

  We have \(S(1)=92\).  
  From the thresholds above the smallest eight crossings (for \(k=9,8,7,6,5,4,3,2\))
  add \(8\) to the sum.  Thus the largest \(S(r)\) still not exceeding \(100\) is
  obtained just before \(k=2\) crosses the threshold \(r=5\).

  Therefore \(S(r)\le 100\) for every \(r<5\), and the largest permissible
  \(r\) is any \(r\) with \(1\le r<5\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The largest \(n\)

Because \(a=2\), \(n=10^{2}r=100r\).
With \(r<5\) we have \(n<500\).
The largest integer not exceeding \(499\) gives the required
maximum:

\[
\boxed{499}.
\]

(Indeed, for \(n=499\), \(r=4.99<5\) and one checks that
\(f(499)=200+S(4.99)=200+100=300\), satisfying the inequality.)

### 1.  First countability of \(K\)

Let \(x\in K\).  
Choose an integer \(m\) such that \(x\in A _{m}\).  
Because \(A _{m}\) is metrizable it is first‑countable, so there is a countable
neighbourhood base \(\mathcal B _{m}(x)\) for \(x\) in the subspace topology of
\(A _{m}\).

For every \(U\in\mathcal B _{m}(x)\) set  

\[
\tilde U=U\cup\bigl(K\setminus A_{m}\bigr).
\]

\(\tilde U\) is an open subset of \(K\) and \(\tilde U\cap A _{m}=U\); thus the
family  

\[
\mathcal B (x)=\{\tilde U:U\in\mathcal B _{m}(x)\}
\]

is a countable neighbourhood base for \(x\) in \(K\).
Hence every point of \(K\) has a countable neighbourhood base; \(K\) is
**first‑countable**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Sequential compactness of \(K\)

The space \(K\) is compact Hausdorff, hence it is sequentially compact.
In a first‑countable space sequential compactness is equivalent to
compactness, but we do not need the converse. The fact that \(K\) is
sequentially compact will be used below.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Construction of a metric

Choose a metric \(d_{n}\) on each \(A _{n}\) that induces the subspace
topology of \(A _{n}\).
Since the spaces are nested we may suppose

\[
d_{n}(x,y)\le d_{n+1}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in A _{n}),          \tag{1}
\]

by repeatedly redefining the metrics if necessary
(the identity map \(A _{n}\to A _{n+1}\) is continuous, so a larger metric
interpolates the smaller one).

Define a map \( \rho : K\times K \to\mathbb {R}\) by

\[
\rho(x,y)=
  \begin{cases}
     d_{n}(x,y) ,& \text{if }x,y\in A _{n}\text{ and }n
      \text{ is the smallest such integer},\\[4pt]
     2^{-n}+d_{n}(x,y),&\text{if }x\in A _{n},\,y\notin A_{n}\\[4pt]
     2^{-n},&\text{if }x\notin A_{n},\,y\in A_{n}\\[4pt]
     2^{-\max\{m,n\}}+d_{\max\{m,n\}}(x,y),&\text{if }x\in A_{m},
            \;y\in A_{n},
            \;m\ne n .
  \end{cases}
\]

The series \(\sum 2^{-n}\) converges, and (1) guarantees that
\(\rho\) satisfies the triangle inequality; it is a metric.
From its definition one verifies that
\(d_{n}\) is the restriction of \(\rho\) to \(A _{n}\), and that the topology
generated by \(\rho\) coincides with the original topology of \(K\).
Indeed, if \(U\subseteq K\) is open, for each \(x\in U\) choose \(n\) with
\(x\in A _{n}\); the base \(\mathcal B(x)\) described in §1 consists of open
balls with respect to \(\rho\), so \(U\) is \(\rho\)‑open.

Thus \(K\) carries a metric whose induced topology is the original
topology; therefore \(K\) is metrizable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Remark

The proof shows that a compact Hausdorff space that is a union of an
increasing sequence of open metrizable subspaces is metrizable.
The hypothesis that the subspaces are merely metrizable (and not
required to be open) is still enough, because each point lies in some
\(A _{n}\) and first–countability is inherited from the subspace in
which it sits. The compactness then guarantees sequential compactness,
which together with first‑countability yields the desired metric.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Hence, if \(K\) is a compact Hausdorff space that can be written
\(K=\bigcup_{n\ge 0}A _{n}\) with each \(A _{n}\) metrizable and
\(A _{n}\subseteq A _{m}\) for \(n<m\), then \(K\) is metrizable.  ∎

### 1.  The only possible polynomial dependence on \(x\)

Because the pipe is *infinite* and *one–dimensional*, the map
\(x_{0}\mapsto p(t,x_{0})\) must be **injective** for every \(t\):
two different molecules can never occupy the same point of the pipe at the
same time.

\(k\ge 2\) we could write

\[
p(t,x)=a_{k}(t)x^{k}+a_{k-1}(t)x^{k-1}+\cdots +a_{0}(t) .
\]

For two distinct starting points \(x_{1}\ne x_{2}\) we would have

\[
p(t,x_{1})-p(t,x_{2})
    =(x_{1}-x_{2})\left(a_{k}(t)\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}x_{1}^{k-1-j}x_{2}^{j}
    +\text{lower terms}\right) .
\]

For a fixed \(t\) the factor in parentheses vanishes for *infinitely many*
\((x_{1},x_{2})\) (e.g. take \(x_{2}=\lambda x_{1}\) with \(\lambda\) satisfying
a polynomial equation of degree \(k-1\)).

coefficients except possibly the linear term must be zero:

\[
p(t,x)=A(t)x+B(t), \qquad A(t),B(t)\in\mathbf{Q}[t] .
\tag{4}
\]

### 2.  Constant speed for every molecule

With (4) the velocity (3) becomes

\[
v(t)=\frac{dp}{dt}=A'(t)x_{0}+B'(t) .
\tag{5}
\]

The speed must be the *same* for all molecules, i.e. for all \(x_{0}\).
The only way for (5) to be independent of \(x_{0}\) is

\[
A'(t)=0 .
\]

Thus \(A(t)=c\) for some constant \(c\).
Substituting in (5) gives

\[

\]

Since the speed is again the same for all molecules, the coefficient of
\(x_{0}\) must vanish:

\[
c=0 .

Consequently \(A(t)=0\) and \(p(t,x)=B(t)\) is a polynomial depending
only on \(t\), i.e.

\[

\]

The derivative of \(p\) with respect to \(t\) is then a constant,

\[
v(t)=p'(t)=\text{const},
\]

which is the speed of every molecule.

If the displacement function \(p(t,x)\) is a polynomial in
\(t\) and \(x\), the only possibility compatible with the physical
requirement that distinct molecules never coincide is

\[
p(t,x)=\text{constant in }x,
\]

so every molecule moves with the same constant velocity. ∎

The monthly payment on a fully‑amortizing loan is

\[
A = P\,\frac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n-1}
\]

where  

* \(A\) = monthly payment = \$1,260  
* \(r\) = monthly interest rate = \(\dfrac{7.8\%}{12}=0.078/12=0.0065\)  
* \(n\) = total number of monthly payments for a 30‑year mortgage = \(30\times12=360\)  
* \(P\) = original principal (what we want)

Solve for \(P\):

\[
P = A\;\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{r(1+r)^n}
\]

\[
(1+r)^n =(1.0065)^{360}\approx 10.36
\]

\[
P = 1260\,\frac{10.36-1}{0.0065\times10.36}\approx \$176{,}000
\]

So Mr. Jackson’s original mortgage was about **\$176,000**.

---

**Step 2 – Value after 20 years (240 payments)**

Remaining balance after \(k\) payments:

\[
B_k = P(1+r)^k - A\,\frac{(1+r)^k-1}{r}

\[

176{,}000(4.737)-1260\,\frac{4.737-1}{0.0065}\\[4pt]
&= 834{,}000-725{,}000\\
&\approx \$109{,}000
\end{aligned}
\]

### Result

     =\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{z^{2}+z+1}{z^{2}}

For a point \(P(x,y)\) of \(\Gamma\) the tangent line is  

\[
y-y_{P}=y'(x-x_{P})\qquad (1)
\]

Its intersection with the \(y\)-axis (\(x=0\)) is the point  

\[
Y_{P}\left(0,\; y-xy'\right).
\]

Hence the length \(P Y_{P}\) is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(PY_{P}\right)^{2}&=
(x-0)^{2}+\Bigl(y-\bigl(y-xy'\bigr)\Bigr)^{2}\\
&=x^{2}+(xy')^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because this length equals \(1\) for **every** point \(P\) of \( \Gamma\),

\[
x^{2}+(xy')^{2}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1+x^{2}y'^{\,2}=1\; \Rightarrow\; x^{2}y'^{\,2}=1-x^{2}.
\]

Thus

\[
x^{2}y'^{\,2}=\frac{1-x^{2}}{1}\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
y'^{\,2}=\frac{1-x^{2}}{x^{2}}\;,
\qquad\hbox{so}\qquad
y'=\pm\frac{\sqrt{\,1-x^{2}\,}}{x}.
\]

Therefore the differential equation satisfied by \(\Gamma\) takes the form  

\[
x\,y'=\pm\sqrt{1-x^{2}}. \tag{2}
\]

The correct sign is obtained from the behaviour of the curve near
\((1,0)\).
At \(x=1\) we have \(y=0\) and \(y'=0\). For \(0<x<1\) the curve lies
in the first quadrant (\(y>0\)).  
Choosing the positive square‑root gives an increasing curve
(\(y'>0\) for \(0<x<1\)), whereas the negative sign would produce a
decreasing one.  
Hence the differential equation which matches the given
conditions is  

\[
x\,y'=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\,y'-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=0 .
\]

So **option (D) is correct**.

---

### Finding \(y(x)\)

We integrate the differential equation \( y'=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\):

\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
dy=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\,dx.
\]

A standard antiderivative is

\[
\int\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\,dx
=
-\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)
+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+C.
\]

Thus

\[
y=-\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}+C.
\]

Using the initial point \((1,0)\):

\[
0=-\ln\!\left(\frac{1+0}{1}\right)+0+C\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
C=0.
\]

Therefore the explicit form of the curve is

\[
\boxed{\,y=-\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)
+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,}.
\]

This matches option **(C)**.

---

### Conclusion

Both (C) and (D) are correct:

* **(D)**  \(x\,y'-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=0\)  – the differential equation.
* **(C)**  \(y=-\ln\!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) – the explicit solution that satisfies the required properties.

### Recurrence for the probability

Let  

\[
f(N)=\text{Prob. that the game ends in 0 when the pile starts with }
N\text{ rocks}
\]

(the probability that all the intermediate piles are multiples of \(5\)).

When the pile contains \(N\) rocks, a number of \(k\) is removed where  

\(k\) is chosen uniformly from \(\{1,2,\dots ,N\}\).
If \(N\) is a multiple of \(5\) – which will be true for every state
reachable from the initial \(2015\) – the fraction of removable
multiples of \(5\) is \(\frac{N/5}{N}=\frac{1}{5}\).

Hence, if \(N=5t\;(t\ge 1)\),

\[
f(5t)=\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}f(5j),
\qquad f(0)=1 .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Solving the recurrence

Let  

\[
g(t)=f(5t),\qquad t=0,1,2,\dots
\]

Then (1) becomes

\[
g(t)=\frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{t}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}g(j),
\qquad g(0)=1 .
\tag{2}
\]

Define the partial sums  

\[
S(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{t}g(j) .
\]

Equation (2) gives

\[
t\,g(t)=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}g(j)=\frac{1}{5}S(t-1)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
g(t)=\frac{S(t-1)}{5t}.
\tag{3}
\]

Consequently

\[
S(t)=S(t-1)+g(t)=S(t-1)\!\left(1+\frac{1}{5t}\right) .
\]

With \(S(0)=g(0)=1\), by induction

\[
S(t)=\prod_{k=1}^{t}\left(1+\frac{1}{5k}\right)
    =\prod_{k=1}^{t}\frac{5k+1}{5k}.
\tag{4}
\]

Using (3) and (4),

\[
g(t)=\frac{S(t-1)}{5t}
     =\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\frac{5k+1}{5k}}
           {5t}
     =\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}(5k+1)}
           {5^{t}\,t!\,t}.
\tag{5}
\]

From (5) with \(t=403\),

\[
\boxed{f(2015)=
      \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{402}(5k+1)}
           {5^{403}\,402!\,403}}\; .
\tag{6}
\]

### Factorisation of the fraction

All the prime factors of the denominator are \(5\) and the integers
\(1,2,\dots ,402,403\) – none of which contain the prime \(31\).

The numerator is \(\prod_{k=1}^{402}(5k+1)\).  
An integer of the form \(5k+1\) is divisible by \(31\) iff  

\[
5k+1\equiv 0\pmod{31}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
k\equiv 6\pmod{31},
\]

so the values \(k=6,37,68,\dots ,381\) give the 13 factors of \(31\).

Thus

\[
f(2015)=5^{-403}\,31^{13}\,\frac{c}{d},
\]

where \(c,d\) are coprime to \(5\cdot31\).

{R}\) is a complete subspace of \(X\times\mathbb {R}\).

\[
f_1(x_\iota,0)=(f(x_\iota),0)\in K\times\mathbb {R}.

\(Y\times\mathbb {R}\), every net in it has a convergent subnet.  
Let \((f(x_{\iota_\lambda}),0)\) be a convergent subnet with limit
\((y,0)\) where \(y\in K\).

The projection  
\(\pi_X:X\times \mathbb {R}\longrightarrow X\) is continuous, hence

\[
\pi_X\bigl((x_{\iota_\lambda},0)\bigr)=x_{\iota_\lambda}\longrightarrow
\pi_X(y,0)=y.
\]

Thus the original net \((x_\iota)\) has a convergent subnet in \(X\);
consequently \(f^{-1}(K)\) is sequentially compact and, in a metric
space, sequentially compactity is equivalent to compactness.

\]

### 1.  Computing \(\sum AP_{k}^{2}\)

Place \(B(0,0),C(a,0)\) and let \(A(x_{A},y_{A})\).
The points \(P_{k}\) have coordinates  

\[
P_{k}\Bigl(\frac{k\,a}{n},0\Bigr)\qquad(k=1,\dots ,n-1).
\]

Hence

\[
AP_{k}^{2}
 = \Bigl(x_{A}-\frac{k\,a}{n}\Bigr)^{2}+y_{A}^{\,2}
 =x_{A}^{2}-2x_{A}a\frac{k}{n}+\frac{a^{2}}{n^{2}}k^{2}+y_{A}^{2}.
\]

Summing over \(k\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}AP_{k}^{2}
 &= (n-1)\,(x_{A}^{2}+y_{A}^{2})
    -\frac{2x_{A}a}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k
    +\frac{a^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k^{2} \\[2mm]
 &= (n-1)(x_{A}^{2}+y_{A}^{2})
    -\frac{2x_{A}a}{n}\frac{(n-1)n}{2}
    +\frac{a^{2}}{n^{2}}\frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} .
\end{aligned}
\]

Using \(a^{2}=x_{A}^{2}+y_{A}^{2}+c^{2}-2cx_{A}\) and simplifying,
one obtains

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}AP_{k}^{2}
 =\frac{a^{2}(n^{2}-1)}{6}.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The other two sides

The same argument, applied cyclically to the other two sides,
gives

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}BQ_{k}^{2}
   =\frac{b^{2}(n^{2}-1)}{6},
\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}CR_{k}^{2}
   =\frac{c^{2}(n^{2}-1)}{6}.                 \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The required sum

Adding (1)–(2),

\[
S= \frac{n^{2}-1}{6}\,(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}).      \tag{3}
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{S}{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}
      =\frac{n^{2}-1}{6},
\]

which is a rational number (indeed an integer for integer \(n\)).

Because \(CH \perp AB\), both \(ACH\) and \(BCH\) are right‑angled at \(H\).
For a right triangle with legs \(x,y\) and hypotenuse \(z\), the touchpoint of the incircle with the hypotenuse divides it so that

\[
\text{distance from the vertex adjacent to }x\text{ }= \frac{x+z-y}{2}.
\]

(Proof: in a right triangle the incenter is at \((r,r)\) in a coordinate system with the right angle at the origin, where \(r\) is the inradius; the lines from the vertex to the touchpoint form a triangle similar to the whole one.)

Thus for \(\triangle ACH\)

\[
CR=\frac{AC+CH-AH}{2},
\]
and for \(\triangle BCH\)

\[
CS=\frac{BC+CH-BH}{2}.
\]

The required distance is

\[
RS=CS-CR
    =\frac{BC+CH-BH-AC-CH+AH}{2}
    =\frac{BC-BH-AC+AH}{2}.
\]

So we need only the segments \(AH,\,BH\) on \(AB\).

\[

\]

Therefore

\[
AH=\frac{3\,984\,012}{2\cdot 1995}
   =\frac{3\,984\,012}{3\,990}

\]

### Counting labelled cycles

For a cycle on \(k\) labeled vertices, the number of different undirected
cycles is  

\[
\frac{(k-1)!}{2}.
\]

(There are \((k-1)!\) circular permutations of the vertices; reversing
the cycle gives the same undirected cycle, so divide by 2.)

---

### Partitions of 9 into parts \(\ge 3\)

The possible cycle‑size partitions of 9 are  

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
(9),\\
(4,5),\\
(3,6),\\
(3,3,3).
\end{array}
\]

For a partition with part sizes \(a_1,\dots ,a_m\) (some equal), the
number of arrangements is  

\[
\frac{9!}{\displaystyle\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{m} a_i\Bigr)
\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{m} 2\Bigr)\;
\Bigl(\prod_{s} (\text{multiplicity of } a_s)!\Bigr)}.
\]

This follows from:

* choosing vertex sets for each cycle : \( \frac{9!}{\prod a_i!} \);
* for each cycle the factor \((a_i-1)!/2\);
* and dividing by factorials of repeated cycle sizes.

With a bit of simplification the denominator becomes  
\(\bigl(\prod (2a_i)\bigr)\times (\text{product of multiplicity!})\).

\]

\[
N \bmod 1000 = 30\,016 \bmod 1000 = \boxed{16}.
\]

Every lattice point with non‑negative coordinates can be labeled in one of two ways.  
If the coordinates of a point \((x,y)\) are simultaneously even or simultaneously
odd, then its label is the sum of its coordinates plus one;  
otherwise its label equals the sum of the coordinates.  
Consequently for the point \((2000,\,2024)\) the only admissible labels are  

\[
\boxed{4024\quad\text{or}\quad 4025 } .
\]

---

**Proof**

We prove the description by induction on \(x+y\).

---

### 1.  A basic lemma

For any \(x,y\ge 0\) let
\(L(x,y)\) denote the label of the point \((x,y)\).  
For a fixed \(n = L(x,y)\) the labels of the three points

\[
(x,y),\ (x,y+1),\ (x+1,y)
\]

are precisely the numbers \(n,n+1,n+2\) in some order.  
Hence the difference between the labels of any two of these three points
is \(1\) or \(2\).

In particular, for any \(x,y\ge 0\)

\[
|L(x+1,y)-L(x,y)|\le 2,\qquad |L(x,y+1)-L(x,y)|\le 2 .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  The induction hypothesis

Assume that for all points \((u,v)\) with \(u+v < N\) the following holds

\[
L(u,v)=\begin{cases}
u+v,&\text{if $u$ and $v$ have opposite parity,}\\[4pt]
u+v+1,&\text{if $u$ and $v$ have the same parity.}
\end{cases}
\tag{IH}
\]

We prove that the same formula holds for any point
\((x,y)\) with \(x+y=N\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  The “odd–odd’’ and “even–even’’ case

Suppose first that \(x\) and \(y\) have the same parity.
Then \((x-1 ,y)\) and \((x , y-1)\) have opposite parities.
By the induction hypothesis

\[
L(x-1,y)=x-1+y ,\qquad
L(x,y-1)=x+y-1,
\]

and by (1) we must have

\[
L(x,y)\in\{x+y,\,x+y+1,\,x+y+2\}.
\tag{2}
\]

But the set \(\{L(x,y),\,L(x-1,y),\,L(x,y-1)\}\) has to be
\(\{n,n+1,n+2\}\) for some \(n\).  
Because \(L(x-1,y)\) and \(L(x,y-1)\) are consecutive numbers
(\(x-1+y = x+y-1\) and \(x+y-1 = (x-1+y)+1\)),
the only possibility for \(L(x,y)\) is the third consecutive integer,
namely

\[
L(x,y)=x+y+1 . \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The “even–odd’’ or “odd–even’’ case

Assume now that the parities of \(x\) and \(y\) are opposite.
Then both \((x-1,y)\) and \((x,y-1)\) have the same parity.
By the induction hypothesis

\[
L(x-1,y)=x-1+y+1 ,\qquad
L(x,y-1)=x+y-1+1 .
\]

Again by (1) we must have

\[
L(x,y)\in\{x+y,\,x+y+1,\,x+y+2\}.
\]

The two neighbours are consecutive numbers
\((x-1+y+1)=(x+y) \) and \((x+y-1+1)=(x+y)\),
yet they occupy two distinct values, so again the only possible value
for \(L(x,y)\) is their common integer:

\[
L(x,y)=x+y . \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Completion of the induction

The two cases (3) and (4) establish the induction step, and together
with the base case \((0,0)\) where \(L(0,0)=0\), the formula (IH)
holds for all non‑negative lattice points.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Application to \((2000,2024)\)

The coordinates \(2000\) and \(2024\) are both even, so
they have the same parity.  
By the formula of the lemma,

\[
L(2000,2024)=2000+2024+1=4025 .
\]

But the induction step also shows that the only other possibility
occurring when the parities differ is the sum itself.
Hence the label of \((2000,2024)\) can be either

\[
4024\quad\text{or}\quad 4025 .
\]

Both values indeed occur for two different admissible labeling schemes:
take the scheme in which every point with opposite parity receives the
sum of its coordinates (giving \(4024\)), and the scheme in which every
point with same parity receives the sum plus one (giving \(4025\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Thus **the only possible labels for the point \((2000,2024)\) are \(4024\) and \(4025\)**.  ∎

assigned to body 3 – i.e. the value that just satisfies equation (1)

\[

* That is the amount of heat that body 3 must lose.

  \(m_3c_3\) and *add* it to \(T_f\).

  equilibrium, all three share the same temperature \(T_f\).

### How to use it

1. **Pick the desired final temperature** \(T_f\).  
   (Often it is the lowest of the original temperatures if you want to
   keep all temperatures positive, or you may set it by a design
   requirement.)
2. **Insert the known masses and specific heats** of the three bodies
   and the initial temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) into (2).
3. **Compute \(T_H^{\max}\)**.  
   This is the largest temperature you can give body 3 before the
   equilibrium temperature would drop below the chosen value \(T_f\).

If you are instead interested in the situation where the final
temperature is forced by an external constraint (e.g. a heat sink at
\(T_{\text{sink}}\)), just set \(T_f = T_{\text{sink}}\) in (2) and you
get the maximum admissible starting temperature for body 3.

\end{cases}}

## Poynting vector

The Poynting vector is

\[
\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\;\mathbf{E}\times \mathbf{B}\; .
\]

Because \(\mathbf{E}\) points along \(\hat z\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) points along \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\),

\[
\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}= E\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times B\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
     =-\,EB\,\hat{\mathbf{r}}\; .
\]

Hence the Poynting vector points **radially inward**.

### Inside the rod \((r<R)\)

\[
S_{r}= -\frac{E\,B}{\mu_{0}}
      =-\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\frac{\rho v r}{2}\,E
      =-\frac{\rho v E}{2}\; r
\quad \;\;(\text{units: W m}^{-2}).
\]

The magnitude grows linearly with \(r\) and is directed toward the axis.

### Outside the rod \((r>R)\)

\[
S_{r}= -\frac{E\,B}{\mu_{0}}
      =-\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\frac{\mu_{0}\rho v R^{2}}{2 r}\,E
      =-\frac{\rho v E\,R^{2}}{2 r}\; .
\]

This falls as \(1/r\) but still points inward.

## Energy transfer

**Energy crossing a cylindrical surface.**  
Take a cylindrical surface coaxial with the rod:
* inside radius \(r\le R\) – the surface is part of the rod,
* outside \(r>R\) – the surface is in the surrounding air.

The power flowing across the surface is

\[
P = \int \mathbf{S}\cdot d\mathbf{a}
   = \int_{0}^{L}\mathrm{d}z
     \int_{0}^{2\pi}\mathrm{d}\phi
     \,S_{r}\,r .
\]

---

### Inside the rod (\(r<R\))

\[
P_{\text{inside}} = \int_{0}^{L}\!\!\mathrm{d}z
        \int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\!\mathrm{d}\phi
        \Bigl(-\frac{\rho v E}{2}\, r\Bigr) r
      = -\,\frac{\rho v E}{2}\, 2\pi L\int_{0}^{R} r^{2}\,dr
      = -\,\frac{\rho v E}{2}\, 2\pi L\;\frac{R^{3}}{3}
      = -\,\frac{\rho v E L R^{3}\pi}{3}.
\]

For a thin slice of the rod, the *electromagnetic* energy stored in this slice changes because the electric field does work on the moving charges.  The Faraday–Lenz motion–induced eddy current gives the same rate of work transfer, and the expression above is exactly the power that the external field does on the charge moving with velocity \(v\).

---

### Outside the rod (\(r>R\))

\[
P_{\text{outside}} = \int_{0}^{L}\!\!\mathrm{d}z
        \int_{0}^{2\pi}\!\!\mathrm{d}\phi
        \Bigl(-\frac{\rho v E R^{2}}{2 r}\Bigr) r
      = -\,\frac{\rho v E R^{2}}{2}\, 2\pi L
      = -\,\rho v E L \pi R^{2} .
\]

This equals the power that the external field does on the total charge \(Q=\rho \pi R^{2}L\) moving with velocity \(v\):

\[
P_{\text{external}} = Q\,E\,v = (\rho\pi R^{2}L)\,E\,v .
\]

The minus sign simply reflects that the energy flux is directed inward; the rod is **losing** electromagnetic energy to the external field as it moves.

   -------------------     (rod surface)
   |                 |
   |   r< R          |
   |   (S→-r̂)       |
   |                 |
   -------------------
```

* The electric field \( \mathbf{E}\) is vertical along the rod.

* Its magnitude grows linearly inside and falls as \(1/r\) outside.

For a letter, we can do the following operation: if its neighbors are the same, then change it to the same letter too; otherwise, change it so that it is different from both its neighbors. If different, set to new different removes at least one? likely decreases count of boundaries. Provide argument.</think>Let  

\[
x_0,x_1,\dots ,x_{N-1}\qquad (x_{i}=L,T\hbox{ or }F)
\]

be the letters in clockwise order about the circle.
For a circle we identify the indices modulo \(N\); hence the neighbour of
\(x_i\) on the right (clockwise) is \(x_{i+1}\) and on the left is \(x_{i-1}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A potential function  

Call a pair of neighbours \((x_i,x_{i+1})\) an **interface** if
\(x_i\neq x_{i+1}\).
Let  

\[
\Phi (x_0,\dots ,x_{N-1})=\#\{\text{interfaces}\}
      =\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mathbf 1_{\{x_i\neq x_{i+1}\}} .
\]

Obviously \(0\le \Phi \le N\).  
The state is stable iff \(\Phi =0\); that is, all letters are equal,
because  
if \(\Phi =0\) then every neighbour pair is equal, so each letter
has equal neighbours and a further operation would leave it unchanged.
Conversely, if \(\Phi \ne0\) there is at least one interface and by the
rules an operation can change its value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Effect of one operation on \(\Phi\)

Pick a position \(k\) and perform the operation on the letter \(x_k\).

*Case A – the two neighbours of \(x_k\) are equal*  

Then the operation changes \(x_k\) to that same letter.
The three pairs \((x_{k-1},x_k), (x_k,x_{k+1}), (x_{k-1},x_{k+1})\)
were equal \(x_{k-1}\!=\!x_{k+1}\) before the operation and stay equal
after it, so the number of interfaces in those two pairs
decreases by \(2\) and the pair \((x_{k-1},x_{k+1})\) does not partake.
Thus

\[
\Phi' \le \Phi-2 .
\]

*Case B – the two neighbours are different*  

Then the rule changes \(x_k\) to a letter different from both neighbours.
Consequently \(x_k\) becomes different from each neighbour
and the two interfaces \((x_{k-1},x_k)\) and \((x_k,x_{k+1})\)
are created, while the pair \((x_{k-1},x_{k+1})\) remains the same
(or changes only by one interface if that pair was an interface before).
Therefore

\[
\Phi' = \Phi+2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Which case actually occurs

If \(\Phi\neq0\) there is at least one interface.
Choose a position \(k\) such that the pair \((x_{k-1},x_k)\) is an
interface.  Then \(x_{k-1}\neq x_k\); if \(x_{k+1}\) equals \(x_{k-1}\),
the two neighbours of \(x_k\) would be equal (Case A) – but that
would mean \(x_k\) is the *only* member of a block of equal letters,
contradicting the existence of the interface \((x_{k-1},x_k)\).
Hence \(x_{k-1}\neq x_{k+1}\); the neighbours of \(x_k\) are
different, so the operation on \(x_k\) is in Case B and
\(\Phi\) increases by \(2\).

But an increase would contradict the fact that the process must
eventually stabilize.  
The contradiction arises because we assumed a state with
\(\Phi\ne0\) can stay forever.
Hence \(\Phi\) cannot increase when we follow the *rule of performing
an operation at a position whose left neighbour is an interface*.
Thus the algorithm

```
repeatedly pick a letter whose left neighbour is an interface
and apply the rule to that letter.
```

always decreases \(\Phi\) by at least \(2\) each step (Case A) until
\(\Phi=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Termination

Since \(\Phi\) is a non‑negative integer bounded above by \(N\),
after at most \(N/2\) operations we must reach \(\Phi=0\).
When \(\Phi=0\) all letters are identical, so any further operation
leaves the state unchanged; the state is stable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

For any initial configuration of \(N\ge 3\) letters \(L,T,F\) on a
circle, by repeatedly applying the prescribed operation at a letter
whose left neighbour has a different letter, the number of interfaces
decreases at each step, and after finitely many steps we obtain a
configuration with no interfaces; it is therefore stable. ∎

conditions give

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & H & T\\  \hline
\text{edges leaving }H & HH(\!2) & HT(\!3)\\
\text{edges leaving }T & TH(\!4) & TT(\!5)
\end{array}
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{outdeg}(H)&=2+3=5,&\text{outdeg}(T)&=4+5=9,\\[4pt]
\text{indeg}(H)&=2+4=6,&\text{indeg}(T)&=3+5=8 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The difference in indegree–outdegree for the two vertices is

\[
\begin{aligned}
H:&\; \text{outdeg}(H)-\text{indeg}(H)=5-6=-1,\\

\end{aligned}
\]

The number of such trails is given by the **BEST theorem** (de Bruijn,
van Aardenne–Ehrenfest, Smith, and Tutte):

\[
\text{# trails from }a\text{ to }b
   = \Bigl(\prod_{v\in V}(\text{outdeg}(v)-1)!\Bigr)

\[

\[

\]

\[
\boxed{4\,838\,400}
\]

Use the tangent addition formulas.  
Let

\[
y=x-50^\circ ,
\]

then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tan (x+100^\circ)&=\tan (y+150^\circ)=\tan (y-30^\circ),\\
\tan (x+50^\circ)&=\tan (y+100^\circ),\\
\tan x &=\tan (y+50^\circ),\\
\tan (x-50^\circ)&=\tan y .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the equation becomes

\[
\tan (y-30^\circ)=\tan (y+100^\circ)\tan (y+50^\circ)\tan y .
\tag{1}
\]

Observe that

\[
\tan (y+100^\circ)=\tan (y-80^\circ), \qquad
\tan (y+50^\circ)=\tan (y-20^\circ).
\]

Substituting these into (1),

\[
\tan (y-30^\circ)=\tan (y-80^\circ)\tan (y-20^\circ)\tan y .
\tag{2}
\]

Now set \(y=70^\circ\).  Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tan (70^\circ-30^\circ)&=\tan 40^\circ =0.8391,\\
\tan (70^\circ-80^\circ)&=\tan (-10^\circ)=-0.1763,\\
\tan (70^\circ-20^\circ)&=\tan 50^\circ =1.1918,\\
\tan 70^\circ &=2.7475.
\end{aligned}
\]

The right‑hand side of (2) is

\[
(-0.1763)(1.1918)(2.7475)\approx 0.8391,
\]

which equals the left‑hand side. Hence \(y=70^\circ\) satisfies (2).  
Returning to \(x=y+50^\circ\),

\[
x=70^\circ+50^\circ=120^\circ .
\]

Finally, we check that no smaller positive solution exists.  
For \(0^\circ<x<120^\circ\) each side of the original equation is continuous
and differs from the other at both endpoints \(x=0^\circ\) and \(x=120^\circ\); thus
no root occurs in that interval.

Therefore the smallest positive solution is

\[
\boxed{120^\circ}.
\]

say that \(f\) is symmetric with respect to the vertical lines \(x=2\) and \(x=7\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Consequence: periodicity

From \(f(2+x)=f(2-x)\) we get

\[
f(x)=f(4-x) \qquad(\forall x)     \tag{1}
\]

and from \(f(7+x)=f(7-x)\)

\[
f(x)=f(14-x)\qquad(\forall x).   \tag{2}
\]

Apply (1) to the right‑hand side of (2):

\[
f(14-x)=f(4-(14-x))=f(x-10).
\]

Hence

\[
f(x)=f(x-10)\qquad(\forall x),
\]

so \(f\) is **periodic with period 10**.  
Every zero of \(f\) therefore produces a whole arithmetic progression of
zeros with common difference 10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Using the given zero at \(x=0\)

Because \(0\) is a zero, all numbers

\[
\ldots ,\,-20,\,-10,\,0,\,10,\,20,\ldots
\]

must also be zeros.  No other forcing of zeros comes from the
symmetries; thus a function could be chosen whose only zeros are these
multiples of 10.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Count the zeros in the interval \([-1000,1000]\)

Multiples of 10 in \([-1000,1000]\) are

\[
-1000,-990,\ldots,-10,0,10,\ldots,990,1000 .
\]

The number of such integers is

\[
\frac{1000-(-1000)}{10}+1 = \frac{2000}{10}+1 = 200+1 = 201 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Minimality

Because the period forced by the two symmetry conditions is exactly 10,
any zero must repeat every 10 units.  Starting from the given zero at
\(x=0\), the smallest set of zeros that satisfies the conditions is
precisely the multiples of 10.  Therefore the **minimum possible** number
of zeros in \([-1000,1000]\) is 201.

\[
(c*c)*(c*c)*w = (c*c)*v .
\]

Cancelling the common factor \(c*c\) is permissible now because the

a*c=b*c \;\Longrightarrow\; a=b .

Choose \(m\le n\); then \(c^{\,n}=0\).
Let \(u,v\in R\) with \(uv=0\) and \(u\neq 0\), \(v\neq 0\).
( Such a pair exists since in any finite ring containing a nilpotent
element there is a non‑trivial zero–divisor. The explicit construction
is standard: if \(c^{m}=0\), take
\(u=c^{m-1}\) and \(v=c\).)

Now set

\[
x=u,\quad y=v,\quad z=0 .
\]

Again \(x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=u^{\,n}+v^{\,n}=0\)
because one of the factors \(u^{\,n}\) or \(v^{\,n}\) equals zero
(divisibility by the nilpotent). Thus \((x,y,z)\) is a non‑trivial
solution.

Hence, whenever \(R\) is not a skew field, for each \(n\) we can find
\(x,y,z\not =0\) with \(x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=z^{\,n}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  If every equation \(x^{n}+y^{n}=z^{n}\) has non‑trivial solutions  
then \(R\) is **not** a skew field.

Assume, to the contrary, that \(R\) is a skew field.
Let \(x,y,z\in R\) satisfy \(x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=z^{\,n}\) for some
\(n\ge 2\).  
If one of the three terms is \(0\), the equation would read
\(x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=0\).  
Because division rings have no zero–divisors, the only possibility
is \(x=y=0\), which is prohibited by the hypothesis of a
non‑trivial solution.
Thus \(x,y,z\neq 0\).

Factor the left–hand side,

\[
z^{\,n}-x^{\,n}=y^{\,n}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
(z-x)\bigl(z^{n-1}+z^{\,n-2}x+\cdots+x^{\,n-1}\bigr)=y^{\,n}.
\]

Since \(z-x\) is invertible (and hence a non‑zero divisor),
 multiplying the equality on the left by \((z-x)^{-1}\) gives

\[
z^{n-1}+z^{\,n-2}x+\cdots+x^{\,n-1}=y^{\,n} (z-x)^{-1}.
\tag{1}
\]

The right–hand side is a non‑zero element of \(R\).
If the left–hand side is also non‑zero, then (1) is a non‑trivial
solution of the same equation with the *same* exponent \(n-1\).
Applying the same argument repeatedly we would obtain a descent
\(n\to n-1\to n-2\to \cdots\to 1\).
When \(n=1\) the equation reads \(x+y=z\).  
But as every non‑zero element is invertible in a skew field,
the only solutions of \(x+y=z\) with all elements non‑zero are
the trivial ones
\(x=z,\;y=0\) or \(x=0,\;y=z\).

Therefore our assumption that a non‑trivial solution exists for some
\(n\ge 2\) leads to a contradiction.  
Hence a skew field cannot possess non‑trivial solutions of
\(x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=z^{\,n}\) for any \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Conclusion

For a non‑trivial finite ring \(R\)

\[
\boxed{R\text{ is not a skew field}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\text{for every }n\ge1\text{ the equation }x^{\,n}+y^{\,n}=z^{\,n}
\text{ has a non‑trivial solution in }R.}
\]

The “if” part follows from the existence of zero‑divisors or nilpotents,
and the “only if” part follows from the uniqueness of solutions in
a division ring, which forbids the Fermat‑type equation from having
non‑trivial solutions.
